A Designated Router (DR) and Backup Designated Router (BDR) organize adjacency and link-state exchange on the segment. They are not automatically the host's default gateway, the best internet exit or a router for every packet.

Eligible interface priority is considered first, then router ID; priority 0 makes a router ineligible. The ordinary election is non-preemptive: a later router with higher priority does not instantly replace a functioning DR.
DROTHER routers normally form FULL adjacencies with the DR/BDR. Two DROTHER routers can legitimately remain 2-WAY with each other. A point-to-point OSPF link has no DR/BDR election.
steps: Record show ip ospf neighbor and show ip ospf interface for every router.
Identify DR, BDR and DROTHER roles from actual output.
Shut the DR's OSPF link in the separate lab; observe the role change and recovery.
Restore the link and explain why the original DR is not guaranteed to reclaim the role immediately.

sections.title: Break an adjacency and repair the cause
body: Change R2's transit network statement from area 0 to area 1 in the simulator, leaving R1 in area 0. The expected adjacency no longer forms on that link. A device can have a working Ethernet link but no working OSPF relationship.
steps: Confirm interfaces are up and transit IPv4 addresses are in the same subnet.
Compare OSPF area, network type and hello/dead intervals on both sides.
Check that the transit interface is not accidentally passive.
Check unique router IDs and matching authentication if configured.
Restore area 0, verify FULL, then verify the learned remote prefix and PC-to-PC traffic.

check.question: Does a FULL neighbor prove every remote application works?
check.answer: No. Verify the learned destination route, return path, host settings, policy and service. Adjacency proves a narrower condition.

sections.title: Understand gateway redundancy separately
body: A PC normally has one default-gateway address. With two gateway routers on the same LAN, a first-hop redundancy protocol provides a shared virtual gateway IP and virtual MAC. The host uses that stable gateway while routers coordinate which one forwards.

For an HSRP example, R1 real address = 192.168.10.2, R2 = .3 and virtual gateway = .1. Hosts use .1. HSRP has active and standby roles; VRRP uses master/backup terminology. Protocol timers and conditions affect takeover, so failover is not necessarily lossless.

Both routers need usable routes toward the destination and a valid return path. Two gateways behind one failed switch or one failed upstream circuit do not solve that common failure. Tracking can reduce a router's priority when an upstream condition fails; changing priority/preemption affects which device takes the role.

For CCNA v1.1, this objective asks you to describe purpose, functions and concepts. The OSPF objective also requires configuration and verification; do not treat merely knowing either name as mastery.
steps: Draw one LAN with two gateways and a remote destination. Label real IPs and the shared virtual IP.
Explain which address belongs in the PC's default-gateway field.
Predict the effect of losing the active router versus losing their shared switch.
Describe the checks needed to prove traffic works after takeover, including routes, NAT/firewall state where applicable and both directions.

check.question: Is the OSPF DR the same thing as an HSRP active gateway?
check.answer: No. DR organizes OSPF adjacency on a broadcast segment. HSRP supplies a resilient first-hop gateway to hosts.

mastery: Configure and verify area-0 OSPFv2 on a two-router link.
Interpret IDs, costs, network types, DR/BDR roles and normal neighbor states.
Explain virtual gateways, failover and remaining shared failure points.

services.title: Make the routed connection useful: addresses, translation and traffic handling
services.objectives: CCNA 4.1–4.9 · NAT, DHCP/DNS, QoS and network operations
services.intro: Routing moves packets, but successful applications also depend on addresses, name resolution, permitted traffic and useful monitoring. Learn each service's job, configure the exam-required functions, and test them separately.

sections.title: DHCP supplies settings; DNS resolves names
body: A DHCPv4 exchange is commonly remembered as Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. A lease supplies a client address and settings such as mask, gateway and DNS. A lease is time-limited; renewal and a correct pool matter.

DNS answers questions about names, including address records. A DHCP server can tell a client which DNS server to use, but DHCP does not itself resolve the website name. A DNS response is not proof that routing or the webpage service works.

check.question: The client has a correct lease but the website name resolves to the wrong server. Which dependency should you fix?
check.answer: The DNS record/settings. Preserve the working DHCP configuration and prove name resolution separately.

sections.title: Configure a local DHCP pool
body: Fresh simulator topology: router G0/0 = 192.168.10.1/24, one switch, client PC set to DHCP, and optional DNS Server = .20/24 gateway .1. Configure the server's DNS service and a lab record before expecting name lookup to work.
Reserve .1–.20 so fixed router/server addresses are outside the lease range. One pool must match the subnet in which the client is obtaining its lease.

commands.label: Router — configure LAN and DHCP service
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
exit
ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.20
ip dhcp pool HOME-LAB
 network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 192.168.10.1
 dns-server 192.168.10.20
end
show ip dhcp pool
show ip dhcp binding
commands.expected: A DHCP client should receive a unique usable .10.x address outside the reserved range, correct /24 mask, gateway .1 and DNS .20.

commands.label: Client verification
commands.text:
ipconfig /all
ping 192.168.10.1
nslookup study.example
commands.expected: Use the client tools available in your simulator. Lease fields prove DHCP settings; the name lookup needs an enabled DNS service and matching record.

steps: Release/renew the lease or select DHCP again on the simulated PC.
Compare the actual lease with the intended network, gateway and DNS.
Inspect the router's bindings and pool availability.
Change the pool's default-router to a wrong subnet in the lab; observe why a valid-looking lease does not prove remote access. Restore it and renew.

sections.title: Relay DHCP across a router; configure a DHCP client
body: In a separate saved lab, put the client in 192.168.10.0/24 and the Server in 192.168.20.0/24. Router interfaces are .10.1 and .20.1; Server is .20.20/24 gateway .20.1. In Server Services, create a DHCP pool for the client LAN: gateway .10.1, mask /24, free range beginning .10.21 and an appropriate DNS server.

A client broadcast is local. The relay on the client-facing router interface carries requests to the remote server and identifies the client network. The server must have the correct pool and a return path. Use either the local-router pool exercise or this remote-server exercise, not both active on the same test LAN.

commands.label: Relay router — client-facing interface
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 192.168.20.20
 no shutdown
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
end
commands.expected: Renew the PC lease; it must belong to .10.0/24, not the server's .20.0/24. Verify both router interfaces and the server's gateway.

commands.label: Separate DHCP-client exercise — interface connected to a lab DHCP provider
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address dhcp
 no shutdown
end
show ip interface brief
show ip route
commands.expected: Use a fresh router/topology for this exercise; this replaces that interface's static address. Confirm the learned address and inspect any supplied/default route rather than assuming one exists.

steps: Remove the helper in the relay lab and renew the client; predict no remote offer.
Restore the helper on the client-facing interface.
If a lease still fails, inspect server service/pool, interface state, return route and filtering.

sections.title: NAT: name the addresses before changing them
body: NAT translates addresses; PAT also uses transport identifiers such as ports to let many sessions share an address. Translation does not create a missing route and does not replace a firewall.
Inside local is the inside host's address before translation. Inside global is the address representing that host to the outside. For this lab, .10.20 can appear outside as 203.0.113.10.

Build a new NAT lab: PC .10.10 and inside Server .10.20 connect through a switch to EDGE G0/0 .10.1/24. EDGE G0/1 = 203.0.113.1/24 connects to PROVIDER G0/0 = 203.0.113.2/24. PROVIDER G0/1 = 198.51.100.1/24 connects to outside Server .100.10 and PC .100.20, both gateway .100.1. These are documentation addresses for a simulated internet, not real internet access.

commands.label: EDGE — base NAT topology setup
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
 no shutdown
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
 no shutdown
exit
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.2
end
commands.expected: Configure PROVIDER's two interfaces with the stated addresses and no shutdown. Configure endpoint masks/gateways and enable HTTP on the servers. Save a clean base file to clone for the next three alternatives.

sections.title: Configure static NAT, a dynamic pool and PAT
body: Use separate copies of the clean base NAT file for each alternative. Global addresses .10, .100 and .101 must be unused. They are on the provider-facing subnet in this simulator example; other designs require upstream routing toward the translation block.

Static NAT is a fixed one-to-one mapping. Dynamic NAT allocates an available global address from a pool; without overload, the pool can run out of simultaneous address mappings. PAT allows multiple inside sessions to share the outside interface address using session identifiers.

commands.label: Alternative A — static mapping, EDGE global configuration
commands.text: ip nat inside source static 192.168.10.20 203.0.113.10
commands.expected: From outside PC 198.51.100.20, request http://203.0.113.10 with HTTP enabled on the inside server. Inspect translations and both paths; whether access is permitted also depends on any configured policy.

commands.label: Alternative B — dynamic NAT pool, EDGE global configuration
commands.text:
access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat pool LAB-PUBLIC 203.0.113.100 203.0.113.101 netmask 255.255.255.0
ip nat inside source list 1 pool LAB-PUBLIC
commands.expected: Generate traffic from inside endpoints toward the outside server. The NAT ACL identifies sources eligible for translation; it is not an interface security ACL. Inspect allocated mappings; two globals do not provide an unlimited pool.

commands.label: Alternative C — PAT, EDGE global configuration
commands.text:
access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
commands.expected: Two inside clients can generate traffic using 203.0.113.1 with distinct session identifiers. Test from endpoints, not only with a ping originating on the EDGE router.

commands.label: Verification — privileged EXEC mode
commands.text:
show ip nat translations
show ip nat statistics
show ip route
show access-lists
commands.expected: Translations generally appear after matching traffic, except configured static entries. An empty dynamic table before a test is not automatically a fault. Correlate inside/outside interface roles, ACL matches, route and service results.

steps: In a clone, reverse an interface's inside/outside role and record the failure.
Restore the correct role and retest a fresh client session.
For a pool test, distinguish pool exhaustion from an incorrect default route.
Explain why a working NAT mapping cannot override an ACL that blocks the application.

sections.title: QoS: walk a packet through a busy connection
body: Imagine a voice call and a large file transfer sharing a 10 Mbps exit. When demand exceeds the exit rate, packets queue or are dropped. QoS changes treatment of selected traffic; it does not manufacture bandwidth or eliminate all delay.

Classify packets into groups using agreed criteria, such as source/service. Mark them with a label such as DSCP. A marking is information for policy; downstream devices must actually apply/trust that policy for useful treatment.

Queue packets when they cannot be transmitted immediately. Scheduling chooses which queue is served next. A bounded priority queue can protect time-sensitive voice while other queues still need service. Congestion can overflow queues; congestion-avoidance policies can drop selected traffic before a queue is completely full.

Policing measures traffic against a rate/burst policy and applies configured actions, often dropping or remarking excess traffic. Shaping buffers/delays traffic to smooth it to a configured average rate; full buffers can still cause drops. Shaping introduces delay and is generally used on output.

For CCNA v1.1, describe classification, marking, queuing, congestion, policing and shaping and their per-hop effects. Platform-specific QoS configuration is beyond what this particular objective's verb requires.

rows: Examine congestion, loss, latency and jitter; priority treatment may help
Excess can be dropped/remarked by its policy
Packets are buffered/delayed to smooth output
Labels do not distinguish the traffic needing preferential treatment
Look at endpoints, remote path and application too

check.question: Which normally delays excess traffic rather than immediately dropping it: shaping or policing?
check.answer: Shaping buffers/delays to regulate output. Policing takes the configured conform/exceed/violate actions, commonly dropping or remarking excess traffic.

sections.title: Verify the supporting operations services
body: Use time, logs and counters to explain events, not only to collect command output. NTP synchronizes clocks; syslog records events; SNMP supports management queries/notifications. A monitoring service does not automatically prevent faults.
In the NAT or service lab, add an NTP-enabled Server at a reachable address such as 192.168.10.20. Confirm its service is enabled before pointing the router at it.

commands.label: Example NTP client — router global configuration then EXEC
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
ntp server 192.168.10.20
end
show ntp associations
show ntp status
commands.expected: A reachable, compatible server and time to synchronize are needed. To practice server mode on a separate supported lab router, configure ntp master 3 and point the client at that router; an unsynchronized lab master is not a trusted real-world time source.

rows: Clients synchronize to servers; stratum describes distance from a reference
Facility identifies message category; severity 0–7 runs most urgent to debugging
Manager queries agents/MIB objects; notifications report events
Simple UDP file transfer, normally port 69 for initial request; no built-in authentication
TCP file transfer with login and separate control/data behavior; traditional FTP is unencrypted

steps: Correlate an interface-down event with timestamps and severity in logs.
Distinguish 'server reachable' from 'service configured and responding'.
For file transfers, verify the result rather than assuming a command's acceptance proves success.

mastery: Configure and verify DHCP client/relay, plus explain DNS.
Configure and test static NAT and dynamic pools; distinguish PAT.
Describe the six QoS behaviors in a real congestion scenario.
Understand and verify supporting operations services at their exam-required depth.

security.title: Apply access rules, predict the result and verify the evidence
security.objectives: CCNA 5.3, 5.6 · Device access and IPv4 ACL configuration/verification
security.intro: Routing decides where a packet could go. Access rules decide whether the packet is permitted at a policy point. Write the intended rule in plain language before turning it into commands.

sections.title: Understand match, order, direction and default
body: A standard IPv4 ACL matches source IPv4 address. An extended ACL can also match destination, protocol and ports. Rules are checked in order and stop at the first match. An implicit deny follows the listed entries.

Inbound/outbound describes the router interface's viewpoint, not a universal direction toward the internet. Inbound on the client-facing interface checks packets arriving from clients before routing them onward.

A wildcard mask identifies address bits that may vary: 0.0.0.255 with 192.168.10.0 covers that /24. A host keyword matches one address. An ACL is normally stateless; it does not automatically learn every session like a stateful firewall.

rows: Web traffic in this HTTP lab

sections.title: Build and prove the unfiltered lab first
body: Fresh topology: one router with G0/0 = 192.168.10.1/24 and G0/1 = 192.168.20.1/24, each connected through a switch. Client = .10.10/24 gateway .10.1. Server = .20.20/24 gateway .20.1; enable HTTP.

With both interfaces up, the router has both LANs directly connected. It needs no static route between these two directly connected networks. Verify ping and http://192.168.20.20 before applying an ACL; otherwise you cannot know whether the rule caused the failure.
steps: Check addresses/masks/gateways and interface state.
Test client → server ping and HTTP.
Write the intended policy: permit client-LAN HTTP to this server; deny other arriving client-LAN traffic.
Predict ping will fail after the rule while the permitted HTTP request should still work.

sections.title: Configure and verify an extended ACL
body: Apply the rule only on the client-facing interface inbound for this exercise. The HTTP request matches the permit. Ping matches the explicit deny. The return server traffic arrives on the other interface and is not checked by this particular inbound ACL.

commands.label: Router — named extended ACL and attachment
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
ip access-list extended LAB-WEB-ONLY
 permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.20.20 eq 80
 deny ip any any
exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip access-group LAB-WEB-ONLY in
end
show access-lists
show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/0
commands.expected: After tests, the HTTP permit and ping deny counters should provide evidence. Existing cache/sessions can confuse tests; create a fresh request and inspect counts.

commands.label: Remove the attachment for a controlled comparison
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 no ip access-group LAB-WEB-ONLY in
end
commands.expected: The ACL definition still exists, but this interface no longer applies it. Retest and compare. Reattach to restore the intended lab policy.

check.question: If deny ip any any appears before the HTTP permit, does the later permit rescue HTTP?
check.answer: No. The first matching deny ends evaluation. Fix the rule order and verify with new traffic/counters.

sections.title: Practice standard ACLs and diagnose placement
body: Clone the unfiltered lab. A standard ACL can distinguish source networks but cannot permit only HTTP to one server. Place it with the intended reachability scope in mind; a broad source-only block near the sender can unintentionally affect many destinations.

commands.label: Standard ACL example — permit this source LAN on server-facing exit
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
access-list 10 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip access-group 10 out
end
show access-lists 10
commands.expected: This permits traffic from the client LAN out this interface and implicitly denies other sources. It does not select a service port. Do not combine it with the extended exercise unless you deliberately want both checks.

steps: Before blaming an ACL, verify routes and server service.
Inspect rule order, source/destination, protocol/port, wildcard and interface direction.
Look for counter increases on the rule you expected to match.
Inspect the return direction and any other policy points.
Repair one rule/attachment at a time; record the evidence before and after.

sections.title: Secure the device and distinguish security functions
body: A local login authenticates the administrator; AAA separates authentication (who), authorization (allowed actions) and accounting (activity records). RADIUS/TACACS+ support centralized AAA; they are not routing protocols.

Use SSH for encrypted remote administration. Telnet and traditional HTTP lack that protection. HTTPS protects browser management when supported. Apply management restrictions without losing the intended administrator's access in the lab.

NAT changes addresses, a router forwards between networks, an ACL applies stateless packet rules, and a stateful firewall tracks sessions. An IPS inspects/prevents selected suspicious traffic. They solve different problems even when bundled in one box.

The broader security topic also covers threats, policy, VPN purpose, wireless authentication and Layer 2 protection. This added walkthrough deepens the requested routing/access-rule area; it does not replace those existing sections.
steps: Use the IOS walkthrough to configure a lab-only local account and SSH.
Test authorized remote access and the effect of a wrong password.
Explain which policy controls management access versus traffic merely passing through the router.
Describe why allowing one service differs from allowing every connection to the server.

mastery: Predict standard/extended ACL matching and rule order.
Configure, attach and verify ACLs with actual lab traffic/counters.
Explain direction, implicit deny, return traffic and device-management security.

ios.title: From the console prompt to a verified router interface
ios.objectives: CCNA 2.8, 4.8, 5.3 · Management access, SSH and local device access
ios.intro: A successful command changes configuration, but it does not prove a working connection. Learn the IOS modes, build a small interface lab, verify it and save only after checking the result.

sections.title: Know where each command belongs
body: User EXEC usually ends in >. enable enters privileged EXEC (#), where show and copy commands are normally available. configure terminal enters global configuration (config)#. interface enters the selected interface's configuration mode.
exit returns one level; end returns to privileged EXEC. ? shows available choices. Interface names vary by router—inspect show ip interface brief before substituting examples.

running-config is the current configuration. startup-config is loaded at boot. copy running-config startup-config saves the current result. A saved wrong setting remains wrong, so verification comes first.

rows: Privileged EXEC: show ip interface brief

sections.title: Bring up a LAN and interpret the state
body: Fresh Packet Tracer router–switch–PC lab: router LAN .10.1/24; PC .10.10/24 gateway .10.1. Use a supported Ethernet interface and connect a working cable.

commands.label: Router console
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
hostname LAB-R1
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description Lab-client-LAN
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
end
show ip interface brief
show running-config
show ip route
commands.expected: up/up indicates the physical/link protocol state is working for this exercise; C/L entries identify the connected network/local interface address. Administratively down means shutdown; down/down can indicate cable/peer/interface problems.

steps: Ping the router from the PC.
Set shutdown deliberately in the simulator and record the changed state.
Use no shutdown to restore it, then compare ping and route output.
Save the verified running configuration; reload only your saved simulator file/device if you want to test persistence.

sections.title: Configure a lab-only account and SSH
body: Use a simulator router supporting SSH/RSA. Substitute your own lab-only password for the placeholder before entering commands. The router needs a hostname, domain name, local account, keys and VTY login settings. Existing account/security settings in a real device need a separate plan; this is a fresh lab.

commands.label: Router — SSH management setup
commands.text:
enable
configure terminal
ip domain-name study.example
username learner privilege 1 secret <choose-a-lab-only-password>
crypto key generate rsa
! Choose 2048 bits if the simulator supports it
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
end
show ip ssh
commands.expected: Key generation is interactive on some simulator models. If the simulated image supports only a smaller key size, that is a simulator limitation, not a real-world security recommendation.

steps: On the lab client, use its SSH client to connect as learner to 192.168.10.1.
Confirm a correct password permits login and a wrong one does not.
Explain why this privilege-1 account cannot automatically perform every privileged operation; authorization matters.
Compare console recovery/initial access with remote access dependencies: working IP path, permitted management port and login settings.
Save the working configuration after verification.

sections.title: Match management methods to the situation
body: Console is useful for initial configuration or recovery without a working IP management path. SSH encrypts command-line remote sessions. HTTPS encrypts supported browser management; plain HTTP and Telnet expose data without that protection.

Cloud management uses a service/control connection and its authentication/policy. TACACS+ and RADIUS can support centralized AAA rather than a locally configured account. Neither replaces the need for a reachable and permitted management path.

check.question: The PC can ping the router but SSH fails. What comes next?
check.answer: Check SSH support/keys, VTY transport and login settings, username/password, TCP 22 policy and the client's SSH settings. Ping success alone does not prove an SSH service is available.

mastery: Choose IOS modes and inspect running/startup configuration.
Configure and verify a LAN interface, then save.
Configure/test SSH in a supported lab and explain management/AAA roles.

routers.introduction: A router joins IP networks. Your default gateway is the local router address a host uses for destinations outside its subnet. A routing table chooses a next hop or exit interface; a default route is used when no more specific route matches. Forward delivery and a return path are both needed.

levels.title: Choose local delivery or the gateway
levels.scenario: PC 192.168.1.10/24 talks to printer 192.168.1.20 and a website outside that subnet.
reasoning: The /24 mask puts both local devices in 192.168.1.0/24.
The printer is reached locally; the remote website is sent through gateway 192.168.1.1.
levels.task: For PC 192.168.5.10/24, classify destinations 192.168.5.25 and 192.168.6.25.
steps: Write the PC subnet.
Compare each destination with it.
State when gateway 192.168.5.1 is used.
levels.hint: With /24, compare the first three octets.
levels.answer: .5.25 is local; .6.25 is remote and needs the default gateway. A gateway is not needed solely for communication inside the same subnet.
levels.check: You choose a gateway based on the destination subnet.

levels.title: Read the first hop
levels.scenario: ipconfig shows gateway 192.168.1.1; tracert shows it first, then an asterisk on a later hop while browsing succeeds.
reasoning: The first responding hop often identifies the local router.
An asterisk means a probe response was not received; filtering or rate limiting can cause this.
Successful browsing is evidence that the application path still works.
levels.task: Inspect ipconfig and tracert example.com on your own Windows PC without changing settings.
steps: Record address, mask, and gateway.
Compare the first responding hop with the gateway.
Write what a timeout does and does not prove.
levels.hint: Routers are not required to answer every diagnostic probe.
levels.answer: A timeout does not by itself prove a broken route. If browsing works, some traffic reaches the service; record the missing probe response separately from application success.
levels.check: Your note avoids treating every asterisk as an outage.

levels.title: Find the missing return path
levels.scenario: Router A reaches LAN B, but PC replies fail because Router B has no route to LAN A.
reasoning: The outward packet and return packet each require routing decisions.
A successful one-direction path does not create a reverse route automatically.
Inspect both routing tables and host gateways before changing anything.
levels.task: On paper, use LAN A 192.168.10.0/24, LAN B 192.168.20.0/24, transit A 10.0.0.1/30 and B 10.0.0.2/30. Supply reciprocal routes.
steps: Write A’s route to LAN B.
Write B’s route to LAN A.
Trace a request and reply, including both PC gateways.
levels.hint: Each next hop is the other router on the transit link.
levels.answer: A: ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.2. B: ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.1. PCs use their own LAN router addresses as gateways. Interfaces and local routes must also be working.
levels.check: You can explain both directions rather than checking only one router.

switches.introduction: An Ethernet switch forwards frames within a VLAN. It learns a source MAC address on the receiving port. A known destination goes to its learned port; an unknown destination or broadcast is flooded to other eligible ports in the same VLAN. This is separate from a router selecting an IP route.

levels.title: Learn the source
levels.scenario: PC A on port 1 sends a frame to PC B on port 2; the switch table is empty.
reasoning: The switch learns A’s source MAC on port 1.
B is unknown, so the frame is flooded within the VLAN except back to port 1.
B’s reply teaches the switch B’s MAC on port 2.
levels.task: Predict the table after two PCs exchange frames.
steps: Draw a switch with two connected PCs.
Write the learned source and port for each transmission.
Predict the port used for the next frame to B.
levels.hint: Learning uses the source; forwarding uses the destination.
levels.answer: After both transmit, A maps to port 1 and B to port 2. The next known unicast frame to B uses port 2.
levels.check: You distinguish learning from forwarding.

levels.title: Observe ARP then ping
levels.scenario: PCs .10 and .11 in 192.168.10.0/24 share a switch. Before pinging, a PC needs its peer’s MAC address.
reasoning: ARP requests use a broadcast on the local VLAN.
The peer replies with its MAC, enabling unicast delivery.
The switch’s MAC table and the host’s ARP table answer different questions.
levels.task: Build the original two-PC Packet Tracer lab and inspect ARP/ICMP in Simulation mode.
steps: Set .10/24 and .11/24, connect both to the same VLAN, and ping.
Inspect the ARP request and reply.
Run show mac address-table and match entries to the actual cables.
levels.hint: The host maps IP to MAC; the switch maps MAC to port.
levels.answer: ARP discovers the destination’s local MAC. The switch learns each transmitting MAC on its incoming port, then forwards known unicast frames to that port. Initial ping attempts may wait for address resolution.
levels.check: You explain the broadcast, reply, and subsequent unicast delivery.

levels.title: Separate MAC movement from a loop
levels.scenario: A MAC moves once after a PC is recabled. Another MAC rapidly alternates ports while the LAN is unstable.
reasoning: A single move can be normal: the switch relearns a source on a new port.
Repeated flapping can indicate a loop or another topology issue; the table alone is not a complete diagnosis.
Inspect cabling and spanning-tree state before blaming the endpoint.
levels.task: Write an investigation for repeated MAC movement on a two-switch lab.
steps: Record the MAC, ports, and timing.
Draw redundant links and inspect show spanning-tree.
Identify a controlled lab test and the result that would support a loop hypothesis.
levels.hint: Look for repeated learning through multiple paths.
levels.answer: Check physical topology, STP roles, and whether a loop is forwarding. In an isolated saved lab, remove one suspected redundant link and compare stability; do not make that change on a live network. Stable relearning after a deliberate recable is different from continuing flapping.
levels.check: You justify the test and preserve alternative explanations.

clients-servers.introduction: A client requests a service and a server supplies it. A browser is a web client. HTTP commonly uses TCP port 80 and HTTPS 443; DNS resolves names and DHCP supplies network settings. Reaching a server’s IP address does not prove that the application you want is running.

levels.title: Identify the roles
levels.scenario: Chrome requests a page from a web server using HTTPS.
reasoning: Chrome is the client, the page-hosting service is the server.
HTTPS protects web communication; its common TCP port is 443.
levels.task: Label a laptop browser opening an HTTP page from 192.168.20.20.
steps: Name the client and server.
Name the service and common port.
Explain why the roles describe software behavior.
levels.hint: One device can host a service and also request another service.
levels.answer: The browser is the client, 192.168.20.20 hosts the web service, and HTTP commonly uses TCP 80. Client and server are roles, not fixed categories of hardware.
levels.check: You identify roles, service, and port.

levels.title: Ping works but the page fails
levels.scenario: A Packet Tracer server answers ping, but its HTTP service is disabled.
reasoning: Ping tests ICMP reachability, not the HTTP application.
A disabled service cannot respond with a page even when the host is reachable.
levels.task: Build PC .10 and Server .20 on 192.168.20.0/24; compare HTTP on and off.
steps: Enable HTTP in Server Services and open http://192.168.20.20.
Disable HTTP and repeat the browser and ping tests.
Record which result changes and why.
levels.hint: Test the service you actually need.
levels.answer: With HTTP enabled the page should load. With it disabled, ping can still succeed while browsing fails. The network and application results must be recorded separately.
levels.check: You diagnose the service without calling it a general network outage.

levels.title: Distinguish name and service failures
levels.scenario: A lab page opens by IP but not by name. Later, the name resolves correctly but the page still fails.
reasoning: IP success with name failure suggests investigating DNS first.
Correct DNS only proves a name-to-address answer, not an available web service.
Check the resolved address, service state, and TCP policy after DNS.
levels.task: Write a test sequence for a named lab website, showing two different failure cases.
steps: Verify the IP-based page.
Use nslookup to compare the answer with the intended lab server.
If resolution is correct, inspect HTTP state and any ACL affecting TCP 80.
levels.hint: Keep name resolution and application connectivity as separate tests.
levels.answer: Case one: investigate a missing/wrong DNS record or client DNS setting. Case two: investigate service state, path, or policy even when DNS answers correctly. Neither result alone identifies the exact fault.
levels.check: Your next test changes when new evidence rules out DNS.

layers.introduction: Layers divide communication into jobs. An HTTP message can be carried by TCP, inside IP, inside an Ethernet frame. IP identifies endpoints across networks; Ethernet MAC addresses deliver on a local link. At a router, the outgoing link gets a new frame. TCP offers ordered reliable transport; UDP leaves delivery guarantees to higher layers.

levels.title: Unpack the layers
levels.scenario: A lab browser sends an HTTP request across Ethernet.
reasoning: HTTP is application content.
TCP carries the application conversation, IP handles network delivery, and Ethernet carries it on the local link.
levels.task: Put Ethernet frame, IP packet, TCP segment, and HTTP message in outside-to-inside order.
steps: Write the four names.
State one responsibility for each.
levels.hint: A frame contains a packet, rather than the other way around.
levels.answer: Ethernet frame → IP packet → TCP segment → HTTP message. Link delivery, routed addressing, transport, and application each serve a distinct job.
levels.check: You explain the order without memorizing only names.

levels.title: Follow addresses across a router
levels.scenario: A PC sends to a server in another subnet through its gateway.
reasoning: The first Ethernet destination is the gateway’s MAC, not the remote server’s MAC.
At the router, the old frame is removed and a new link frame is built.
Without NAT, the endpoint IP addresses remain while link MAC addresses change.
levels.task: Sketch PC, router, and remote server; label the first and second frames.
steps: Give each link its own MAC labels.
Keep the PC and server IP labels consistent.
Explain how the PC resolves its gateway MAC using ARP.
levels.hint: MAC addresses are for the current Ethernet link.
levels.answer: First frame: PC MAC to gateway MAC. Outgoing frame: router outgoing MAC to the next local receiver MAC. The packet still targets the server IP, assuming no NAT.
levels.check: You distinguish local link addresses from end-to-end IP addresses.

levels.title: Diagnose bottom-up
levels.scenario: A lab cable is unplugged; DNS and HTTP tests both fail.
reasoning: Layer 1 loss prevents the dependent higher layers from communicating.
Changing DNS cannot restore an unplugged link.
After restoring the link, verify addressing, reachability, and the service rather than assuming every fault is gone.
levels.task: Create a layered investigation for a page failure with link down, then link up but HTTP disabled.
steps: Check the link first and record its state.
After link restoration, test IP reachability.
Test the page and identify the remaining application failure.
levels.hint: A successful repair at one layer does not prove all layers work.
levels.answer: First repair the lab link. Then verify address/gateway and IP reachability. If ping succeeds but the HTTP service is off, enable the service in the lab and retest; the second fault is application-related.
levels.check: You identify two faults with distinct evidence.

addressing-basics.introduction: An IPv4 address and mask identify a subnet and a host within it. A /24 mask is 255.255.255.0. In 192.168.10.0/24, .0 is the network, .255 is broadcast, and .1–.254 are ordinary host addresses. Hosts send local traffic directly and remote traffic through a gateway reachable on their LAN.

levels.title: Recognize valid hosts
levels.scenario: 192.168.10.10/24 and .11/24 are valid hosts in the same subnet.
reasoning: The network is .0 and broadcast is .255.
The different host addresses can communicate locally when the link/VLAN is correct.
levels.task: Find the network, broadcast, and usable range for 192.168.7.25/24.
steps: Apply the /24 mask.
List the first and last usable addresses.
Choose a valid gateway address.
levels.hint: A gateway is normally another usable host address in that subnet.
levels.answer: Network 192.168.7.0, broadcast 192.168.7.255, hosts .1–.254; .1 is a possible gateway if actually configured on the router.
levels.check: You avoid assigning network or broadcast addresses to hosts.

levels.title: Check a /26 boundary
levels.scenario: 192.168.10.70/26 belongs to the block .64–.127.
reasoning: A /26 has 64 total addresses.
Network .64 and broadcast .127 leave hosts .65–.126.
levels.task: Decide whether 192.168.10.60/26 and .70/26 are local peers.
steps: Write the /26 block size.
Find each network boundary.
State whether routing is needed.
levels.hint: The blocks start at 0, 64, 128, and 192.
levels.answer: .60 is in .0/26; .70 is in .64/26. They are in different subnets and need routing despite sharing the first three octets.
levels.check: You use the mask rather than only comparing address appearance.

levels.title: Spot an unreachable gateway
levels.scenario: A host is 192.168.10.100/27 with gateway .65.
reasoning: /27 blocks contain 32 addresses.
.100 belongs to .96/27, hosts .97–.126.
.65 is in .64/27 and is not an ordinary locally reachable gateway for this host.
levels.task: Audit host .150/27, gateway .129, and peer .158/27.
steps: Find the host subnet and usable range.
Check gateway and peer membership.
Propose one valid correction if gateway .129 is the actual router address.
levels.hint: Determine the block before making changes.
levels.answer: .150/27 is in .128/27, hosts .129–.158, broadcast .159. Gateway .129 and peer .158 are valid members; no correction is required. The task tests whether you can verify a good configuration rather than invent a fault.
levels.check: You can explain why this configuration is valid and the earlier one is not.

firewalls-basics.introduction: A firewall decides which traffic is allowed. Read a rule by source, destination, protocol, port, and direction. A stateful firewall also tracks connections so replies can be permitted. NAT translates addresses; it does not replace a deliberate traffic policy. Inspect your live PC settings only; make experiments in an isolated lab.

levels.title: Read one connection rule
levels.scenario: A client connects to a server on TCP 443.
reasoning: 443 is the server’s destination service port for common HTTPS traffic.
The return packet has the server as source and the client as destination.
levels.task: Write a rule description allowing a client to a web server on TCP 443.
steps: Name source and destination.
Name protocol and destination port.
State the intended direction.
levels.hint: Specify the intended service rather than all traffic.
levels.answer: Allow the client source to the web-server destination using TCP destination port 443 in the direction of the request.
levels.check: Your rule identifies the exact flow.

levels.title: Interpret stateful replies
levels.scenario: A stateful firewall permits an outbound HTTPS session and its established return traffic.
reasoning: The initiating rule allows the intended session.
Connection state distinguishes replies from unrelated unsolicited inbound traffic.
levels.task: Compare an established HTTPS reply with a new inbound connection from an unknown host.
steps: Draw the original request and its reply.
Label a separate unsolicited request.
Describe the difference in expected policy.
levels.hint: Being inbound does not mean every packet is a new inbound session.
levels.answer: The established reply can be permitted by state tracking. A new unsolicited session needs its own policy permission; it is not automatically accepted because outbound HTTPS is allowed.
levels.check: You explain state without saying every inbound packet is allowed.

levels.title: Handle a policy exception
levels.scenario: Staff need HTTPS to one server; management needs SSH; ordinary staff must not reach management services.
reasoning: Separate service requirements into distinct rules.
Order and scope matter; broad permits can undermine specific restrictions.
Test an allowed and denied flow for every intended boundary.
levels.task: Build a written policy table for staff, web server, and management networks.
steps: List HTTPS and SSH requirements with exact source/destination groups.
Add a default-deny policy and explain reply handling for a stateful firewall.
Write positive and negative tests, including staff-to-SSH.
levels.hint: Do not treat address translation as your deny rule.
levels.answer: Allow staff → web server TCP 443; allow management → administered devices TCP 22; deny other new traffic by default. Established replies follow state policy. Verify HTTPS works, management SSH works, and staff SSH is denied; document any required supporting services separately.
levels.check: You can justify every permit and test the restriction.

first-troubleshooting.introduction: Troubleshooting narrows a fault with evidence. Start with who is affected and what fails. Then check link, address, local gateway, remote path, DNS, and application. A ping failure alone is not proof of an outage because ICMP can be filtered. Record observations before changing configuration.

levels.title: Find the scope
levels.scenario: One laptop fails; other devices on the same connection browse normally.
reasoning: The issue is not affecting every client.
Start with the affected laptop’s link and settings instead of rebooting all equipment.
levels.task: Write three scope questions for a customer who says “the internet is down.”
steps: Ask which devices are affected.
Ask whether wired and Wi-Fi differ.
Ask whether one site or every service fails.
levels.hint: Questions should separate possible causes.
levels.answer: Useful questions identify device scope, connection type, and application scope. Ask what changed and when it began next.
levels.check: Your questions narrow the fault rather than guessing a repair.

levels.title: Interpret DNS evidence
levels.scenario: Gateway ping works, a lab site opens by IP, and nslookup of its name fails.
reasoning: Local connectivity works for the tested path.
An IP-based web request works, so investigate name resolution.
Check the configured DNS server and the intended record.
levels.task: Write a support note for those three results.
steps: State issue and scope.
List each test and result.
Choose the next DNS check without changing the live connection.
levels.hint: A note needs evidence, not just “DNS broken.”
levels.answer: Issue: named lab website fails. Evidence: gateway responds; page opens by IP; lookup fails. Next: inspect client DNS configuration and query the intended DNS server for the record. This points toward DNS but does not yet identify server versus client configuration.
levels.check: Your conclusion is limited to what the tests establish.

levels.title: Avoid a misleading ping
levels.scenario: Gateway and website pings fail, but HTTPS browsing works on the same PC.
reasoning: ICMP and HTTPS are different traffic types.
Browsing proves an application connection works; ping can be filtered.
Select a test for the reported symptom rather than forcing every probe to succeed.
levels.task: Diagnose a complaint where one HTTPS site fails, three others work, and all pings time out.
steps: Record which applications work.
Check the failing name’s DNS response and browser error.
Choose a service/path test and an escalation note without asserting a total outage.
levels.hint: Filter the evidence by the actual service.
levels.answer: Investigate the affected site’s name, service, certificate/browser error, or specific path/policy. The working sites contradict a complete internet outage. Ping timeouts alone do not resolve the site-specific fault.
levels.check: You reconcile apparently conflicting results and propose a focused next test.

ios.introduction: Cisco IOS has user EXEC, privileged EXEC, global configuration, and interface configuration modes. show commands inspect state; configuration commands change it. An administratively down interface is disabled in configuration. Running configuration is active now; startup configuration is used after a restart. Use console access and an isolated Packet Tracer lab for these exercises.

levels.title: Read the interface state
levels.scenario: show ip interface brief lists GigabitEthernet0/0 as administratively down/down.
reasoning: The interface is disabled by configuration.
no shutdown enables it, but the link still needs a connected peer and working cable.
levels.task: Inspect a Packet Tracer router and identify its connected interface.
steps: Enter enable, then show ip interface brief.
Match the interface to the topology cable.
Explain administratively down versus up/up.
levels.hint: The exact interface name depends on the router model.
levels.answer: Administratively down means disabled locally. up/up means the physical and line-protocol states are up. Enabling alone does not guarantee up/up.
levels.check: You choose the actual connected interface rather than copying an unrelated name.

levels.title: Configure and save a gateway
levels.scenario: A PC is 192.168.1.10/24 and the router must be 192.168.1.1.
reasoning: The router address must be on the PC LAN.
Configure the connected interface, enable it, verify, and save.
levels.task: Bring up a lab router gateway for PC 192.168.2.10/24.
steps: Set PC gateway 192.168.2.1.
On the router enter enable; configure terminal; interface <connected-interface>; ip address 192.168.2.1 255.255.255.0; no shutdown; end.
Run show ip interface brief, ping from the PC, and copy running-config startup-config.
levels.hint: Replace <connected-interface> with the actual interface name; enter each command separately.
levels.answer: The connected interface should have .2.1 and become up/up with a working link. The PC should reach it. Saving copies the current configuration to startup configuration.
levels.check: You verify both interface state and host reachability before saving.

levels.title: Find two independent mistakes
levels.scenario: A router has the wrong LAN address and is administratively down; enabling it alone does not repair the address.
reasoning: A single symptom can hide multiple errors.
Compare intended addressing with running configuration, then examine operational state.
Retest after each repair and save only the verified result.
levels.task: In a saved lab, configure gateway .3.1/24 as .4.1/24 and shut it down, then diagnose from PC .3.10/24.
steps: Use show ip interface brief and show running-config.
Correct the IP on the actual connected interface and enable it.
Verify gateway ping and running/startup configuration after saving.
levels.hint: An up interface can still have incorrect addressing.
levels.answer: Restore 192.168.3.1/24, no shutdown, and correct the PC gateway to .3.1 if needed. Confirm up/up and ping; copy running-config startup-config. Both the shutdown state and wrong subnet explain distinct parts of the failure.
levels.check: You document both faults and prove the saved configuration matches the repair.

subnetting.introduction: A prefix leaves host bits: /26 leaves six, so it has 64 total addresses and normally 62 usable hosts. Subnet blocks must start on valid boundaries. VLSM uses different block sizes for different needs; allocate the largest requirement first. Count required router interfaces as hosts too. The ordinary minus-two rule has /31 and /32 exceptions.

levels.title: Calculate a /26
reasoning: 32−26 = 6 host bits; 2^6 = 64 total addresses.
Reserve network .0 and broadcast .63, leaving .1–.62.
levels.task: Calculate network, broadcast, and hosts for 192.168.50.64/26.
steps: Use block size 64.
Add 63 to the network to find broadcast.
Remove the first and last addresses from the host range.
levels.hint: The next block begins at .128.
levels.answer: Network .64, broadcast .127, hosts .65–.126, 62 usable.
levels.check: All boundaries and host counts agree.

levels.title: Fit three departments
levels.scenario: A /24 must hold total requirements of 60, 30, and 12 usable addresses.
reasoning: 60 fits /26 (62 usable), 30 fits /27 (30 usable), and 12 fits /28 (14 usable).
Allocate the largest block first, then place smaller blocks on valid boundaries.
levels.task: Plan those three blocks inside 192.168.50.0/24 and choose gateways.
steps: Allocate /26, /27, then /28.
List network, host range, and broadcast for each.
Choose gateway addresses from the usable ranges; state whether gateways are included in the requirements.
levels.hint: A requirement of 30 PCs plus one gateway needs more than 30 usable addresses.
levels.answer: .0/26: hosts .1–.62, broadcast .63; .64/27: hosts .65–.94, broadcast .95; .96/28: hosts .97–.110, broadcast .111. Gateways can be .1, .65, and .97. This plan assumes the given counts include all required interfaces.
levels.check: You detect overlap and explicitly account for gateway consumption.

levels.title: Detect an impossible budget
levels.scenario: A /24 must support 100, 60, 30, and 14 end devices, each group also needing a gateway.
reasoning: Host needs become 101, 61, 31, and 15.
They need blocks of 128, 64, 64, and 32 addresses respectively.
288 total addresses exceed a /24’s 256; a clever ordering cannot make it fit.
levels.task: Explain why the request cannot fit and propose a valid larger allocation on paper.
steps: Choose the smallest prefix per group.
Add the block sizes.
Allocate inside 192.168.50.0/23 and check boundaries.
levels.hint: Do not subtract gateway needs from the device counts.
levels.answer: Use .50.0/25 (126 usable), .50.128/26 (62), .50.192/26 (62), and .51.0/27 (30) inside 192.168.50.0/23. Their broadcasts are .50.127, .50.191, .50.255, and .51.31. They do not overlap. A /23 gives room for all four.
levels.check: You reject an impossible /24 and justify a valid replacement.

ipv6.introduction: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written as eight hexadecimal groups. Remove leading zeros within a group and use :: once for a consecutive run of zero groups. Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6 instead of IPv4 ARP; there is no IPv6 broadcast. Use 2001:db8::/32 documentation addresses in examples and a /64 for these lab LANs.

levels.title: Compress an address
reasoning: Leading zeros inside a group can be removed.
The four consecutive all-zero groups are represented by one ::.
steps: Remove leading zeros.
Replace the zero run once.
Count back to eight groups to verify.
levels.hint: You cannot use two :: sequences in one address.
levels.answer: 2001:db8:2::11. Expansion restores eight groups.
levels.check: You can expand your compressed result unambiguously.

levels.title: Build the IPv6 LAN
levels.scenario: Router ::1 and PCs ::10 and ::11 use 2001:db8:1::/64.
reasoning: They share a /64 and can communicate locally.
The router must have an IPv6 address on its connected interface; routing between LANs also requires IPv6 routing.
levels.task: Add IPv6 to a working Packet Tracer IPv4 LAN.
steps: On the router enable ipv6 unicast-routing and set ipv6 address 2001:db8:1::1/64 on the connected interface.
Set PC IPv6 addresses 2001:db8:1::10/64 and ::11/64; use the lab router as gateway as the simulator supports.
Ping locally and inspect show ipv6 interface brief and show ipv6 neighbors.
levels.hint: Neighbor Discovery supplies link-layer neighbor information; it is not ARP.
levels.answer: With links up and correct settings, local pings work. The neighbor table can show discovered link-layer peers. A /64 prefix is shared, but each endpoint has its own address.
levels.check: You verify addressing and neighbor discovery rather than assuming IPv4 settings carry over.

levels.title: Diagnose mismatched prefixes
levels.scenario: PC A is 2001:db8:1::10/64; PC B was accidentally set to 2001:db8:2::11/64 on the same isolated LAN.
reasoning: The physical link does not make different IP prefixes the same subnet.
With no routing to the second prefix, end-to-end traffic fails.
Link-local connectivity can differ from global-prefix connectivity.
levels.task: Repair the saved dual-stack lab and describe what IPv4 success proves.
steps: Compare the IPv6 /64 prefixes on both PCs and router.
Restore B to 2001:db8:1::11/64 and retest.
Explain why working IPv4 did not validate IPv6 addressing.
levels.hint: Treat the two protocol configurations separately.
levels.answer: IPv4 success supports working link and IPv4 configuration; it does not prove IPv6 is correct. Restoring B’s intended /64 resolves this prefix error when other settings and policy are correct.
levels.check: You identify the IPv6-specific fault without reconfiguring working IPv4.

vlans.introduction: A VLAN is a separate Layer 2 broadcast domain. An access port serves one ordinary data VLAN; a trunk carries multiple VLANs with 802.1Q tagging. Same-VLAN hosts across switches need that VLAN on both switches and the trunk. Different VLAN subnets need routing and correct gateways. A VLAN is not itself an access-control policy.

levels.title: Place two teams
levels.scenario: Sales uses VLAN 10, support uses VLAN 20.
reasoning: Put each PC access port in the intended VLAN.
Broadcasts in VLAN 10 are not simply forwarded into VLAN 20.
levels.task: On a Packet Tracer switch, put two PCs in VLAN 10 and a third in VLAN 20.
steps: Create vlan 10 and vlan 20 in global configuration.
On each connected PC port enter switchport mode access and switchport access vlan <10-or-20>.
Use show vlan brief to match ports and VLANs.
levels.hint: Replace the placeholder with 10 or 20; match the actual interface.
levels.answer: The two team-10 PC ports belong to VLAN 10; the third belongs to VLAN 20. Same-subnet addressing is needed for same-VLAN IP tests; inter-VLAN delivery needs a router.
levels.check: The port assignments match the topology.

levels.title: Carry both VLANs between switches
levels.scenario: Each of two switches has a VLAN 10 PC; a trunk connects the switches.
reasoning: Both switches need VLAN 10 present.
The trunk must carry VLAN 10 for same-VLAN traffic across the link.
levels.task: Extend the lab to two switches with VLANs 10 and 20.
steps: Create both VLANs on both switches and set PC access ports.
On both ends of the inter-switch link set switchport mode trunk and switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20.
Run show interfaces trunk; test same-VLAN PCs on different switches using matching subnets.
levels.hint: A PC access port and an inter-switch trunk have different jobs.
levels.answer: VLAN 10 peers should communicate across the trunk, as should VLAN 20 peers, with correct addressing and links. Different VLANs still need routing; trunking alone does not route.
levels.check: You verify each VLAN independently and do not expect a trunk to replace a router.

levels.title: Repair a selective outage
levels.scenario: VLAN 10 works across switches; VLAN 20 works locally but fails across the trunk because it was omitted from an allowed list.
reasoning: Local VLAN 20 success narrows attention to its inter-switch path.
Compare allowed and active trunk VLANs on both ends.
Restore VLAN 20 while retaining VLAN 10.
levels.task: Remove VLAN 20 from one lab trunk, diagnose it, and restore it.
steps: Save a working baseline and introduce the omission.
Collect show vlan brief and show interfaces trunk evidence.
Restore switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20 and retest both VLANs.
levels.hint: Use the full intended allowed list; do not accidentally replace VLAN 10.
levels.answer: The omitted VLAN cannot cross that trunk even though its local access ports work. Restoring both intended VLANs repairs the selective trunk fault. For inter-VLAN traffic also verify router subinterfaces, dot1Q tags, and gateways.
levels.check: You repair the specific VLAN and confirm no regression in the other.

stp.introduction: Redundant Layer 2 links can create loops. Spanning Tree chooses a loop-free active topology and leaves an alternate path available. The lowest bridge ID wins root election. EtherChannel groups compatible physical links into one logical link; LACP negotiates membership. Use show spanning-tree and show etherchannel summary to verify actual behavior.

levels.title: Predict the root
levels.scenario: Three switches have different bridge priorities: 4096, 8192, and 32768 for VLAN 10.
reasoning: Lower priority contributes to a lower bridge ID.
With these distinct priorities, the 4096 switch wins for VLAN 10.
levels.task: Choose the root from priorities 8192, 16384, and 32768.
steps: Rank the priorities.
Explain the tie-breaker if priorities match.
Verify the lab result with show spanning-tree vlan 10.
levels.hint: MAC address breaks a bridge-ID tie when the other components match.
levels.answer: 8192 wins among these priorities. With equal priority/system-ID extension, the lowest MAC decides. Check the actual VLAN instance rather than assuming one root for all VLANs.
levels.check: You justify the election and read the reported root.

levels.title: Observe a failover
levels.scenario: A triangle of switches has an alternate blocked/discarding path.
reasoning: STP keeps redundant paths from all forwarding simultaneously.
When an active link fails, topology can reconverge through an alternate path.
levels.task: Build a three-switch triangle in Packet Tracer with consistent VLANs/trunks.
steps: Inspect show spanning-tree on each switch.
Record root and port roles/states before failure.
Remove one active lab link, wait for convergence, and compare pings and roles.
levels.hint: Expect convergence behavior, not guaranteed zero packet loss.
levels.answer: The remaining topology should regain connectivity if a valid alternate path exists. Port roles/states change; transient loss can occur. Record actual timings instead of asserting instant failover.
levels.check: Your before/after diagram matches the observed forwarding paths.

levels.title: Diagnose a channel mismatch
levels.scenario: One switch uses LACP active; its peer uses passive. Another pair uses passive on both sides.
reasoning: Active initiates LACP and can pair with passive.
Two passive ends do not initiate negotiation, so a channel is not negotiated.
VLAN, speed, and other member settings must also be compatible.
levels.task: On a separate lab pair, compare active/passive with passive/passive.
steps: Configure matching trunk settings on two member ports at both ends.
Use channel-group 1 mode active on one end and passive on the other; inspect show etherchannel summary.
Change the active end to passive and compare; restore active/passive.
levels.hint: An unformed channel is not automatically a loop; STP still governs independent links.
levels.answer: Active/passive can negotiate; passive/passive does not initiate. Verify that ports are actually bundled and that the logical port-channel is correct. Do not infer success solely from entered commands.
levels.check: You explain the negotiation difference and confirm bundle state.

routing.introduction: A routing table lists reachable prefixes and next hops. Forwarding uses the longest matching prefix. For competing sources advertising the same prefix, administrative distance helps choose the source. A default route is /0. A floating static route has a higher distance than the primary route and only helps when that primary route is withdrawn or tracked appropriately.

levels.title: Pick the specific route
levels.scenario: A table has 0.0.0.0/0 via A and 192.168.20.0/24 via B.
reasoning: 192.168.20.10 matches both.
The /24 is more specific than /0, so B is selected.
levels.task: Choose next hops for 192.168.20.25 and 192.168.30.25.
steps: Compare both destinations with the /24.
Use the default for the one with no specific match.
levels.hint: Longest prefix wins among installed matching routes.
levels.answer: .20.25 uses B; .30.25 uses A, assuming those are the only installed matches and their next hops are usable.
levels.check: You apply prefix specificity before other comparisons.

levels.title: Configure reciprocal static routes
levels.scenario: Two routers join LANs .10.0/24 and .20.0/24 through 10.0.0.0/30.
reasoning: Transit addresses .1 and .2 are direct next hops.
Each router needs a route to the other LAN, and each PC needs its local gateway.
levels.task: Build the two-branch Packet Tracer topology from the original lab.
steps: Set router A transit 10.0.0.1/30 and B 10.0.0.2/30 and enable links.
Inspect show ip route and ping between PCs using their respective LAN gateways.
levels.hint: The destination prefix is the remote LAN; the next hop is the neighboring router.
levels.answer: Both remote LAN routes should be installed with reachable next hops. End-to-end success requires working LAN interfaces, host settings, and both directions.
levels.check: You trace request and reply using both tables.

levels.title: Combine specificity and backup routes
levels.scenario: The table contains .20.0/24 and .20.128/25; the /25 points to a path that is not delivering traffic.
reasoning: A destination .20.150 uses /25 even if /24 has a lower distance.
The router does not automatically try the less-specific /24 because an application fails.
Route withdrawal or tracking must change the installed forwarding choice.
levels.task: Explain next-hop choices for .20.100 and .20.150, and a safe lab recovery plan.
steps: List which prefixes match each host.
Choose the longest match.
Inspect the /25 next hop and route availability; repair or remove the faulty lab-specific route, then retest.
levels.hint: Distance does not override different prefix lengths during forwarding.
levels.answer: .100 uses /24; .150 uses /25. Repair the /25 path or withdraw the faulty specific route in the lab so an appropriate remaining route can match. A higher-distance same-prefix backup helps only under the route’s actual withdrawal/tracking conditions.
levels.check: You avoid claiming a more general route automatically rescues a failing more specific route.

ospf.introduction: OSPF dynamically exchanges routes between neighboring routers. Adjacent links need compatible area, subnet, and protocol settings. The process number is locally significant; it need not match between routers. Verify neighbors and learned routes separately. For a simple lab use a point-to-point link in area 0; gateway redundancy is a separate function.

levels.title: Read an OSPF route
levels.scenario: show ip route includes an O-prefixed remote LAN route.
reasoning: O indicates a route learned through OSPF.
The route’s next hop is a neighboring router, not the final PC.
levels.task: Explain an O route to 192.168.20.0/24 via 10.0.0.2.
steps: Name the source protocol.
Name destination prefix and next hop.
State what host settings still matter.
levels.hint: A learned route does not set a PC gateway.
levels.answer: OSPF learned .20.0/24 through neighbor 10.0.0.2. PCs still need valid addresses, masks, and local gateways; return routing and policy must work.
levels.check: You read the entry without confusing next hop and endpoint.

levels.title: Form a two-router adjacency
levels.scenario: Routers A and B use transit .1 and .2 in 10.0.0.0/30, area 0.
reasoning: Enable OSPF on the transit and LAN interfaces.
Verify adjacency, then verify the remote LAN route.
A process number identifies a local process.
levels.task: Replace the static routes in the saved two-branch lab with OSPF.
steps: Remove only the two lab static routes; configure router ospf 1 on each router.
A: network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0 and network 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 area 0; B uses the same transit and its .20.0 LAN.
Run show ip ospf neighbor and show ip route, then test between PCs.
levels.hint: Network statements select local interfaces; they are not static next-hop routes.
levels.answer: With compatible link settings, neighbors form and remote LAN routes appear as OSPF routes. A local process-ID mismatch alone is not the cause of an adjacency failure.
levels.check: You verify neighbors, routing entries, and host traffic as three separate checks.

levels.title: Repair an area mismatch
levels.scenario: One transit interface is in area 0 and the peer is in area 1; adjacency does not form.
reasoning: Peers on the shared link need matching areas.
Confirm interfaces, addresses, areas, timers, and passive settings with evidence.
Correct the intended area rather than changing every setting.
levels.task: Introduce the area mismatch in your saved lab, then diagnose it.
steps: Inspect show ip ospf interface on the transit interfaces.
Remove the incorrect network statement and add the area 0 statement.
Wait for convergence; verify neighbor state, learned LAN routes, and PC pings.
levels.hint: Fix the shared link area; the process ID need not match.
levels.answer: Restore the peer transit interface to area 0 using the intended statement/interface configuration. Retest all three checks. Other mismatches can also block neighbors, so an area match is necessary but not universal proof of success.
levels.check: Your evidence identifies the area fault and confirms recovery.

services.introduction: DHCP gives clients addresses, masks, gateways, and DNS settings. DNS maps names to records. A DHCP relay forwards client requests across a router because broadcasts do not normally cross it. NAT translates addresses; PAT also uses transport ports to share an address. Test address assignment, DNS resolution, and the application separately.

levels.title: Read a lease
levels.scenario: DHCP supplies 192.168.10.25/24, gateway .1, and DNS 192.168.20.20.
reasoning: The address/mask determines the local subnet.
The gateway reaches other networks and the DNS server resolves names.
levels.task: Label the job of each field in that lease.
steps: Write the local subnet.
Explain why the DNS server can be on a different routed subnet.
State what a wrong gateway would affect.
levels.hint: DNS and gateway are separate settings.
levels.answer: Local subnet .10.0/24; gateway .10.1 routes remote traffic; DNS .20.20 resolves names if reachable through routing/policy. A wrong gateway can break remote DNS and other remote services while local peers still work.
levels.check: You identify each field’s role.

levels.title: Relay a remote DHCP request
levels.scenario: Client LAN is 192.168.10.0/24; DHCP Server is 192.168.20.20/24 behind a router.
reasoning: The client broadcast stays local unless a relay forwards it.
Set the helper on the client-facing interface.
The server pool must match the client subnet and supply its gateway.
levels.task: Build the two-LAN service lab with router addresses .10.1 and .20.1.
steps: Set server .20.20/24 with gateway .20.1.
Create a server DHCP pool for .10.0/24, gateway .10.1, DNS .20.20, and a free client address range.
On router’s client interface use ip helper-address 192.168.20.20; select DHCP on the client and inspect its lease.
levels.hint: Do not put the helper only on the server-facing interface.
levels.answer: The client receives a .10.x lease with the .10.1 gateway. The relay identifies the client network to the server. Correct server return routing, enabled services, and policy are also required.
levels.check: The lease belongs to the client subnet, not the server LAN.

levels.title: Separate three service faults
levels.scenario: A client gets a correct lease; its named page fails because DNS points to the wrong server. After correction, HTTP is still disabled.
reasoning: A correct lease rules out some DHCP errors.
Compare the resolved address with the intended web server.
Then test the actual web service; DNS success is not application success.
levels.task: In the lab, add a wrong DNS A record and disable HTTP; repair both with evidence.
steps: Record the lease and query the intended DNS server.
Correct the record to the lab web server address.
Enable HTTP and compare name lookup, IP-based browsing, and named browsing.
levels.hint: Use a lab-only name such as study.example and keep it consistent.
levels.answer: First correct the DNS record; then restore HTTP. Record that address assignment worked throughout. Final checks should show a correct lease, the intended DNS answer, and a working web page by IP and name.
levels.check: You report distinct faults instead of saying “DHCP/DNS/NAT is broken.”

wireless.introduction: Wireless access proceeds through association, authentication, IP configuration, and onward connectivity. An SSID is the Wi-Fi name. A passphrase permits joining; an administrator password controls router settings. Use WPA2-Personal where supported in Packet Tracer; real devices may also support WPA3. GHz frequency and cellular 5G are different concepts.

levels.title: Separate the passwords
levels.scenario: A laptop joins StudyWiFi with a Wi-Fi passphrase; the router uses a different admin password.
reasoning: Joining and administration are different permissions.
Correct SSID and security settings are needed to authenticate.
levels.task: Create a lab SSID and identify the two credentials without using real passwords.
steps: Set StudyWiFi with WPA2-Personal in Packet Tracer.
Use an invented lab passphrase and join the laptop.
Explain which credential controls configuration.
levels.hint: Never reuse a real password in a shared lab file.
levels.answer: The Wi-Fi passphrase joins clients; the administrator password controls settings. Joining does not establish a working DHCP lease or internet path.
levels.check: You distinguish joining from administration and browsing.

levels.title: Compare authentication and DHCP faults
levels.scenario: Wrong passphrase prevents authentication; a disabled DHCP service can leave an authenticated client without a valid lease.
reasoning: These failures happen at different stages.
Inspect association/authentication before interpreting IP settings.
levels.task: Compare a wrong passphrase and disabled DHCP in a saved wireless lab.
steps: With DHCP enabled, try a wrong passphrase and record the join result.
Restore the passphrase, then disable lab DHCP and renew/reconnect the client.
Restore DHCP and verify the address/gateway and a local service.
levels.hint: An old lease can persist, so inspect/renew rather than assuming a blank address.
levels.answer: A password failure prevents a valid join. A DHCP failure affects settings after joining, though an existing lease can mask it. Restoring both should give the intended subnet and local connectivity.
levels.check: You identify the failing stage from observed evidence.

levels.title: Wi-Fi works, upstream fails
levels.scenario: A laptop reaches the lab router and a local server, but cannot reach a remote server after a route is removed.
reasoning: Local wireless and IP delivery work for the tested services.
Investigate routing/policy beyond the local network instead of changing the passphrase.
Compare a wired client to the same remote service.
levels.task: Remove one remote lab route and build a troubleshooting note.
steps: Test local gateway and service from wireless and wired clients.
Inspect the router’s remote and return routes.
Restore the intended route and verify remote service access on both clients.
levels.hint: Use a simulated remote server; Packet Tracer does not provide actual internet service.
levels.answer: If both clients share the remote failure while local service works, a common upstream fault is plausible. Restore the missing route in the lab and retest both directions. The working local tests do not prove every radio metric is ideal, only the tested connectivity.
levels.check: Your investigation follows the failing path rather than resetting Wi-Fi.

security.introduction: An access control list (ACL) evaluates traffic in order; the first matching entry decides. An implicit deny catches unmatched traffic. Extended IPv4 ACLs can match source, destination, protocol, and ports. Direction is relative to the router interface. A normal IOS interface ACL is not automatically a stateful firewall. Test allowed and denied flows in a saved isolated lab.

levels.title: Apply the first match
levels.scenario: An ACL permits TCP to server 192.168.20.20 port 80, then denies other IP traffic.
reasoning: A matching HTTP request is permitted.
ICMP ping does not match the TCP permit and is denied.
levels.task: Predict HTTP, HTTPS, and ping results under this two-rule policy.
steps: Identify each protocol/port.
Walk through rules top to bottom.
Name the first match for each flow.
levels.hint: HTTPS 443 is different from HTTP 80.
levels.answer: HTTP to the specified server is permitted; HTTPS and ping are denied. Unspecified flows do not inherit the HTTP permission.
levels.check: You explain every result through a rule match.

levels.title: Permit a lab web service
levels.scenario: Client LAN .10.0/24 needs HTTP to server .20.20 across a router.
reasoning: An inbound client-facing ACL evaluates requests as they enter the router.
Create all intended entries before applying it.
This exercise deliberately denies other traffic, including ping.
levels.task: Build a named ACL in Packet Tracer after confirming the baseline page works.
steps: In global configuration: ip access-list extended STUDY; permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.20.20 eq 80; deny ip any any; exit.
On the actual client-facing interface apply ip access-group STUDY in, then end.
Open http://192.168.20.20, try ping, and inspect show access-lists.
levels.hint: Use the server IP so this HTTP-only test does not depend on a DNS permit.
levels.answer: HTTP should pass and ping should be denied under this policy, assuming working routes and HTTP. Response traffic enters the server-facing interface; evaluate any other ACLs there separately. A normal ACL is not state tracking.
levels.check: You verify a permitted and denied test with counters and correct interface direction.

levels.title: Repair a shadowed permit
levels.scenario: deny ip any any appears above the intended HTTP permit.
reasoning: Every IP packet matches the broad deny first.
The later permit cannot be reached for that traffic.
Removing the broad deny altogether can conceal missing policy; restore intended order.
levels.task: In a saved lab, put the deny first, then diagnose and repair the rule order.
steps: Use show access-lists and compare hit counters after a browser test.
Detach the lab ACL from the interface while rebuilding it in the correct order using console access.
Apply the completed ACL again; confirm HTTP allowed and ping denied.
levels.hint: Keep the specific permit ahead of the catch-all deny.
levels.answer: Rebuild STUDY with the TCP 80 permit first and the deny second, then reapply inbound on the client interface. Confirm routes/service remain intact. No return-session allowance is implied by a standard stateless ACL.
levels.check: Your repair preserves the restriction rather than permitting all traffic.

architecture.introduction: A network design connects roles and failure boundaries. Access switches connect endpoints, routers connect subnets, and firewalls enforce policies. The data plane forwards traffic, control plane determines forwarding information, and management plane supports administration. Virtual machines and containers host workloads; a controller helps coordinate configuration but is not necessarily in the data path.

levels.title: Label a small office
levels.scenario: PCs use a switch, phones use an AP, and a router/firewall reaches the ISP.
reasoning: The access devices connect local endpoints.
The router connects networks and the firewall controls traffic.
levels.task: Draw that office and label each role.
steps: Include PCs, switch, AP, gateway, access device, and ISP.
Mark Ethernet and Wi-Fi links.
Identify where IP routing and policy decisions occur.
levels.hint: Multiple roles can share one physical device.
levels.answer: The switch/AP provide local access; gateway routes remote packets; firewall applies policy; modem/ONT handles the provider access link. Combined equipment should retain role labels.
levels.check: Your drawing distinguishes functions rather than just listing boxes.

levels.title: Separate two teams
levels.scenario: Staff and guests use separate VLANs and subnets; guests should reach only the intended external services.
reasoning: Routing makes inter-subnet connectivity possible.
A policy restriction must deliberately limit guest access.
DHCP, DNS, and management placement need explicit consideration.
levels.task: Draw a two-VLAN office and a local staff server.
