steps: Assign two non-overlapping /24s and gateways.
Label trunks, access ports, DHCP/DNS, and the server.
Write staff-to-server and guest-to-server expected outcomes.
levels.hint: VLAN separation alone does not enforce every routed restriction.
levels.answer: One possible design: staff .10.0/24 gateway .10.1; guests .20.0/24 gateway .20.1. Staff can reach the service by policy; guests are denied that local server. Document allowed DHCP/DNS and external paths so the guest network is usable.
levels.check: Both topology and traffic policy support the stated design.

levels.title: Choose justified redundancy
levels.scenario: An office has one switch, one gateway, and one ISP circuit. A second AP fixes none of those three failures.
reasoning: Match each improvement to a failure it actually protects against.
Redundant gateways still require a valid downstream and upstream design.
Two circuits through one failed gateway can still be unavailable.
levels.task: Choose two failure scenarios and design a remedy plus a failover test for each.
steps: Mark the single points of failure.
Specify which devices/links survive each failure.
Describe what may still interrupt service and how to verify recovery in a lab or on paper.
levels.hint: Redundancy is about independent working paths, not the number of boxes.
levels.answer: Examples: redundant gateway pair with first-hop redundancy addresses one gateway failure when paths remain; separate access switches and suitable connections address a switch failure for connected clients. A second ISP helps circuit failure only when routing/failover and gateway availability also support it.
levels.check: Each remedy maps to a specific failure and includes a verifiable test.

automation.introduction: Automation describes desired changes through structured data and repeatable actions. JSON has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. HTTP GET typically reads; PATCH requests a partial change as the API defines. Authentication, schema validation, scope, a before/after check, and rollback matter. AI suggestions require verification against actual device state.

levels.title: Read JSON types
levels.scenario: An interface record is {"name":"Gi0/0","enabled":true,"mtu":1500}.
reasoning: name is a string, enabled a boolean, and mtu a number.
The string "true" is not the same JSON type as true.
levels.task: Write a JSON object for Gi0/1, disabled, MTU 1500.
steps: Use double-quoted property names and string values.
Use false without quotes.
Check commas and braces in a JSON-aware editor.
levels.hint: JSON does not allow trailing commas or comments.
levels.answer: {"name":"Gi0/1","enabled":false,"mtu":1500}. Correct syntax and types are distinct from whether a device API accepts these field names.
levels.check: Your JSON parses and you explain each value type.

levels.title: Plan a partial change
levels.scenario: A fictional API allows PATCH /interfaces/Gi0-1 with {"enabled":true}.
reasoning: Read current state with GET first.
PATCH changes one field according to this fictional API contract.
Read again and verify actual state instead of treating a successful request as the only check.
levels.task: Write a no-credentials, paper workflow to enable one lab interface.
steps: Record the target and current state.
Write the intended PATCH body and expected response check.
Describe the follow-up GET and rollback to the recorded state.
levels.hint: The URL and schema here are illustrative, not a real router endpoint.
levels.answer: GET current record; validate target/schema; PATCH enabled=true; check response; GET state and verify link behavior. Roll back enabled to its recorded value if needed. Never send this fictional endpoint to a live device.
levels.check: Your workflow limits the change to one intended target and verifies it.

levels.title: Reject unsafe bulk changes
levels.scenario: An AI-produced inventory includes a duplicate interface and enabled values mixing strings with booleans.
reasoning: A parser can accept syntactically valid JSON that violates the intended schema.
Validate types, duplicates, target allowlist, and allowed fields before making changes.
Use a dry run and a small verified batch; do not blindly apply the proposal.
levels.task: Design validation for [{"name":"Gi0/0","enabled":true},{"name":"Gi0/0","enabled":"false"}].
steps: Identify duplicate target and wrong type.
Write rejection messages for both.
Describe a corrected preview and before/after verification plan.
levels.hint: Do not silently convert or overwrite the conflicting record.
levels.answer: Reject the duplicate Gi0/0 and string "false"; require one unambiguous record with a boolean. Review the intended target, back up state, preview changes, apply only in a lab, and verify before increasing scope.
levels.check: Invalid data stops the change instead of producing a partial hidden result.

capstone.introduction: A capstone combines the earlier skills into one network. Establish a working baseline, define allowed/denied traffic, then introduce faults one at a time before attempting mixed faults. Use evidence to decide whether the cause is addressing, VLAN/trunk, routing, service, or policy. Planner completion is a study record; compare your understanding with current official exam objectives.

levels.title: Prove the baseline
levels.scenario: Two branches exchange pings and a client opens a lab HTTP server.
reasoning: List the expected path before introducing faults.
Verify local gateway, remote host, and application separately.
levels.task: Save a two-branch baseline from your earlier labs.
steps: Record host addresses, gateways, VLANs, and routes.
Test local and remote reachability and HTTP.
Save the Packet Tracer file and a short results table.
levels.hint: A baseline needs observed results, not only a topology drawing.
levels.answer: The saved baseline should have expected connectivity with documented settings. State any intentional blocked tests, so a denied ping is not later mistaken for a new fault.
levels.check: You can reproduce the working state and identify expected restrictions.

levels.title: Repair one known fault at a time
levels.scenario: A PC’s wrong gateway breaks remote access while same-subnet traffic remains possible.
reasoning: Local and remote tests distinguish the scope.
Compare the host gateway with the configured local router.
Restore one setting and verify the expected change.
levels.task: Introduce a bad gateway, then a missing trunk VLAN, one at a time in separate saved copies.
steps: Predict affected flows before each change.
Collect host and switch evidence relevant to the fault.
Repair and verify all baseline tests before the next fault.
levels.hint: Return to a known good baseline between experiments.
levels.answer: Wrong gateway mainly affects remote paths; a missing trunk VLAN breaks that VLAN across the trunk. Repairs should address the wrong setting, preserve unrelated settings, and restore the recorded baseline tests.
levels.check: Your notes connect symptom, evidence, specific repair, and retest.

levels.title: Resolve multiple faults without guessing
levels.scenario: A remote page fails because one VLAN is missing from a trunk and an ACL denies its HTTP request.
reasoning: The first repair can expose a second fault.
Verify each segment and then the actual application/policy.
Stop when allowed and denied tests match the design, not when one ping succeeds.
levels.task: In a saved isolated capstone, introduce a trunk omission, a wrong gateway, and a shadowed HTTP permit.
steps: Build a test matrix by source, destination, and service.
Diagnose and repair each fault using show commands and host tests; record each observed change.
Retest required traffic and prohibited traffic, then rebuild the main configuration without notes.
levels.hint: Use the prior VLAN, addressing, and ACL worked examples as reference when needed.
levels.answer: Restore the intended trunk VLAN list, each host’s local gateway, and ACL order with the HTTP permit before the deny. Confirm correct routing/services too. Keep a three-part note for each fault and demonstrate that forbidden flows remain blocked.
levels.check: You diagnose all faults, justify the order, and verify policy as well as reachability.

linux.introduction: Linux support starts with observing addresses, listening services, and logs. ip addr shows addresses; ss -lnt shows listening TCP sockets. Wireshark lets you inspect traffic you own. A service bound to 127.0.0.1 accepts local connections only. Use an isolated VM for these exercises; operating-system menus and commands can vary.

levels.title: Identify a listening service
levels.scenario: ss -lnt lists 127.0.0.1:8000 as LISTEN.
reasoning: The service listens on TCP 8000.
127.0.0.1 is loopback, so the service is local to that host.
levels.task: In an isolated Linux VM with Python 3, start a local page service.
steps: Run python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 from a folder containing only lab files.
In another terminal run ss -lnt and open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in the VM browser.
Stop the service with Ctrl+C when finished.
levels.hint: Do not serve a folder containing personal files.
levels.answer: A listening entry appears for loopback port 8000 and a local browser can connect. Stopping the process removes that listener. This does not prove remote accessibility.
levels.check: You match the process, listener, and local request.

levels.title: Distinguish a stopped service
levels.scenario: A local request works before the server stops and fails afterward; the VM address is unchanged.
reasoning: The network configuration did not need to change.
The missing listener supports an application/service fault.
levels.task: Compare listener and browser results before and after stopping your lab HTTP process.
steps: Record ss -lnt while serving.
Stop the process and repeat the command and browser request.
Write a note naming the evidence for the service failure.
levels.hint: A browser error alone gives less evidence than a browser result plus socket state.
levels.answer: Before: loopback TCP 8000 listens and the page opens. After: no listener and the request fails. Restarting the lab service should restore both observations without changing IP settings.
levels.check: You identify a service-state fault rather than changing the gateway.

levels.title: Capture the local conversation
levels.scenario: A VM’s local HTTP request uses loopback; capturing only its Ethernet adapter misses that conversation.
reasoning: Choose the interface carrying the test traffic.
Plain HTTP permits inspecting the lab request; HTTPS would encrypt its content.
Correlate packets with listening state and the browser result.
levels.task: Capture your own loopback HTTP request in Wireshark inside the isolated VM.
steps: Use the loopback interface and filter tcp.port == 8000.
Request the page with the service running and inspect connection setup and HTTP.
Stop it, retry, and compare with ss -lnt; stop the capture when done.
levels.hint: Packet visibility depends on selecting the right capture interface and permissions.
levels.answer: The working capture normally shows TCP setup and an HTTP exchange. A stopped local service can yield a reset rather than a successful connection; record the actual behavior. No packets on the wrong adapter is not proof that the request never occurred.
levels.check: You correlate process state, traffic, and application evidence.

python.introduction: Python can validate repeatable inventory data. The standard-library ipaddress module parses addresses; invalid input raises ValueError. A set can identify repeated normalized addresses. Git records source versions, but should not contain credentials or private device inventories. Work with invented lab data and document how to run the script.

levels.title: Validate one IPv4 address
levels.scenario: ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.10.25") succeeds; "192.168.10.999" raises ValueError.
reasoning: An IPv4 octet must fit its allowed numeric range.
Parsing is more reliable than checking only for dots.
levels.task: Try both inputs in a local Python 3 session.
steps: Run import ipaddress.
Run ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.10.25").
Run the invalid input and explain the ValueError.
levels.hint: A valid address is not proof that a device owns it or is reachable.
levels.answer: The first input parses as an IPv4Address. The second is invalid. The parser validates address form; reachability requires a separate network test.
levels.check: You separate input validation from network availability.

levels.title: Report duplicates and invalid rows
levels.scenario: An inventory has two hosts with .10.25 and a third with .10.999.
reasoning: Catch ValueError per row so one invalid address does not stop the whole report.
Store each successfully parsed address in a set to identify reuse.
levels.task: Write a script over three invented hostname/address pairs using that data.
steps: Parse each address with ipaddress.IPv4Address in a try/except ValueError block.
For valid entries check membership in a seen set before adding.
Print a useful message naming invalid and duplicate rows.
levels.hint: Normalize addresses by parsing before comparing; do not overwrite an earlier record silently.
levels.answer: The script should report one repeated valid address and one invalid row while processing all three. A repeated address is a conflict candidate; document whether duplicates are allowed by the intended inventory model.
levels.check: The report names the problem rows and continues after invalid input.

levels.title: Validate subnet membership too
levels.scenario: For a /26 LAN .64–.127, .64 and .127 are reserved, .70 is usable, and .130 belongs elsewhere.
reasoning: Syntax validation alone accepts all four as IPv4 addresses.
Check network membership and reserved endpoints for this ordinary LAN.
Produce separate reasons so a rejected row is understandable.
levels.task: Extend the inventory validator for 192.168.10.64/26 and those four entries.
steps: Parse the network with ipaddress.ip_network and each row with IPv4Address.
Check membership, then network_address and broadcast_address, then duplicates.
Record sample expected results and save the script/README in a local Git project without secrets.
levels.hint: These reserved-host rules apply to this /26 exercise; /31 and /32 require different treatment.
levels.answer: .70 is usable; .64 is the network; .127 is broadcast; .130 is outside the subnet. Distinguish these failures from malformed input and duplicate usage. Include a run command and example output in the README.
levels.check: Your validation explains four distinct categories and can be rerun reproducibly.

enterprise.introduction: Enterprise networking builds on reliable subnetting, switching, routing, and troubleshooting. Deeper routing and resiliency are useful next skills once the core labs are comfortable. Here the progression is a practical branch-network design, not a claim that these exercises alone cover a professional certification.

levels.title: Add a third subnet
levels.scenario: Two branches use .10.0/24 and .20.0/24; a third can use .30.0/24.
reasoning: Branch LANs must not overlap.
Give the new branch a gateway and a path to the other branches.
levels.task: Draw a third branch using 192.168.30.0/24.
steps: Choose a router LAN address and one PC address.
Add a non-overlapping transit subnet to the existing design.
Trace traffic to branch one and the reply.
levels.hint: Every transit link also consumes an address block.
levels.answer: One valid choice is gateway .30.1 and PC .30.10/24. A new 10.0.0.4/30 transit uses .5 and .6 if that block is free. Supply reciprocal routing or consistent dynamic routing.
levels.check: You account for both LAN and transit address space.

levels.title: Learn routes to the new branch
levels.scenario: The third branch joins an area-0 OSPF lab and advertises its LAN.
reasoning: Adjacency requires compatible shared-link settings.
All branches need the new route and a return path.
levels.task: Extend the capstone to a third router with a free /30 link.
steps: Configure its LAN/transit and hosts.
Enable OSPF on intended links in the existing area-0 lab.
Verify neighbors and learned prefixes, then test each branch pair.
levels.hint: Seeing one neighbor does not prove every LAN is advertised.
levels.answer: Remote branches should learn .30.0/24; the new branch should learn existing LANs. Test each direction and inspect missing-prefix cases rather than assuming adjacency is sufficient.
levels.check: All intended branch pairs work and routes explain the observed path.

levels.title: Design and prove an alternate path
levels.scenario: Three routers form a triangle so a branch can survive one transit-link failure.
reasoning: A physically separate path only helps when routing can use it.
Compare the routing table and application behavior before and after a link loss.
A second path does not protect the failed router itself.
levels.task: Add a separate transit link and test one link failure in the isolated lab.
steps: Allocate a free transit subnet and enable compatible OSPF.
Record the selected routes and successful branch tests.
Shut one transit interface in the lab, observe convergence, and verify recovery; restore it afterward.
levels.hint: Expect convergence and possible transient loss, not uninterrupted delivery by assumption.
levels.answer: If the remaining topology stays connected and advertises the LANs, OSPF can use the alternate path. Record actual convergence and route changes; acknowledge that a router or LAN failure is a different scenario.
levels.check: Your resilience claim is limited to the failure you actually tested.

security-path.introduction: Defensive security applies least privilege, secure administration, logging, and evidence-based incident triage. Start by documenting required flows between client, server, and management networks. Default deny requires explicit supporting services and an understanding of return traffic. These written policy exercises do not require purchasing a certification or changing a live firewall.

levels.title: Write one least-privilege rule
levels.scenario: Staff need HTTPS to an internal server, not every service on it.
reasoning: The service requirement is narrower than all IP traffic.
Record source, destination, protocol, port, and action.
levels.task: Write a table row for staff HTTPS access to 192.168.20.20.
steps: Choose an invented staff subnet.
Specify TCP destination port 443.
State why an unrestricted permit is unnecessary.
levels.hint: Least privilege permits the stated task and no more than required.
levels.answer: For example: source 192.168.10.0/24, destination 192.168.20.20, TCP 443, allow. Other requirements need their own documented justification.
levels.check: Your permit matches a concrete service need.

levels.title: Separate administration
levels.scenario: Management may SSH to devices; ordinary clients may not.
reasoning: Management access requires its own source scope.
A positive SSH test and a negative client SSH test validate different policy requirements.
levels.task: Create a written policy with staff, server, and management networks.
steps: Add staff HTTPS and management SSH rows.
Describe default deny, logging, and stateful return handling if applicable.
List allowed and denied test flows.
levels.hint: Do not assume a stateless ACL handles return sessions like a stateful firewall.
levels.answer: Document staff→server TCP 443 and management→devices TCP 22, plus required DNS/DHCP as appropriate. Deny unrelated new connections. Tests include permitted staff HTTPS, permitted admin SSH, and denied ordinary-client SSH.
levels.check: The table includes both functional access and restrictions.

levels.title: Triage a suspicious blocked attempt
levels.scenario: Logs show many blocked management-port attempts; no successful management session is demonstrated.
reasoning: Denied attempts are evidence of attempts, not proof of a successful compromise.
Correlate source, time, target, authentication events, and actual session state.
Preserve evidence and escalate according to the defined scope.
levels.task: Write a short incident note using only those observations.
steps: Separate observed facts from hypotheses.
Name two additional logs/checks needed to assess success or impact.
Describe containment review without disabling all business access.
levels.hint: Avoid reporting a confirmed breach from deny logs alone.
levels.answer: Record repeated blocked attempts, affected targets/times, and unknown success/impact. Check authentication/session and device-change logs, confirm policy behavior, preserve records, and escalate to the responsible security team if indicated. Any containment change should target the supported risk.
levels.check: Your note neither minimizes the attempts nor invents a confirmed compromise.

cloud-path.introduction: Cloud networks also use subnets, route tables, and traffic policies. A route toward an internet gateway is one requirement, not proof that a workload is publicly reachable. Address assignment and provider-specific security controls also matter. ISP/NOC support similarly separates customer LAN, access circuit, provider path, and service symptoms. These exercises are diagrams, not paid cloud provisioning.

levels.title: Map the support boundary
levels.scenario: A customer phone reaches the router over Wi-Fi; the router reaches the provider through an ONT.
reasoning: The phone/AP/router segment is local.
The access circuit and provider network form a different troubleshooting scope.
levels.task: Draw that path and mark what a customer can observe versus what may require ISP checks.
steps: Label each device/function.
List local join/address/gateway observations.
List circuit/provider evidence to request when escalating.
levels.hint: Do not claim access to provider equipment from the customer LAN.
levels.answer: Customer checks can establish local Wi-Fi/IP/service symptoms. Provider staff may need to verify access-link alarms, provisioning, and upstream paths. A clear escalation includes scope, timing, and local test results.
levels.check: You identify responsibility boundaries without guessing a provider fault.

levels.title: Design public and private cloud subnets
levels.scenario: A diagram uses .10.0/24 for a public-facing tier and .20.0/24 for a private tier.
reasoning: Non-overlapping subnets require intentional routes and policies.
A route to an internet gateway alone does not establish public reachability.
A private workload may use a controlled outbound mechanism without accepting unsolicited inbound access.
levels.task: Draw a provider-neutral virtual network without creating resources.
steps: Mark subnets, route-table association, and service roles.
Show intended inbound/outbound paths and access rules.
List provider-specific details you would verify before implementation.
levels.hint: Public IP assignment and security behavior differ by platform.
levels.answer: Document the public tier’s addressing, internet route, and policy together. Keep the private tier’s inbound access restricted and show any intended outbound NAT/proxy path. Verify current provider behavior before provisioning; this diagram does not certify a deployed configuration.
levels.check: Your design treats route, address, and policy as separate requirements.

levels.title: Choose an evidence-based NOC escalation
levels.scenario: All customers in one area lose remote service while local LAN tests still work; an access alarm is reported.
reasoning: The broader scope supports a shared access/upstream hypothesis.
Local success does not identify the exact provider device that failed.
Combine timing, affected area, alarm, and comparative tests in the handoff.
levels.task: Write an escalation contrasting that case with one failing Wi-Fi client in a working household.
steps: State facts and likely investigation scope for each.
List evidence needed from customer and provider sides.
Choose one skill/project to deepen based on the case you want to handle.
levels.hint: State what is unknown rather than inventing optical measurements.
levels.answer: Area-wide case: escalate shared access/upstream investigation with time, scope, alarm reference, and local results. Single-client case: inspect that client’s join/IP and compare wired/other wireless clients first. A useful next project could be a documented fault-isolation lab or a simulated monitoring dashboard with invented data.
levels.check: You choose different next actions for different scopes and support them with evidence.

Easy.q: What is the main job of a router?
o: Connect different IP networks and forward packets.
Forward frames within one LAN using a MAC table.
Resolve website names to IP addresses.
Easy.h: Review the explanation of this role or action in the lesson. Compare what each choice claims before retrying.

Easy.q: Why is data broken into packets?
o: One message reserves the connection until all its data finishes.
Different devices can take turns using the connection.
Every message gets its own physical connection.
Easy.h: Review the explanation of this role or action in the lesson. Compare what each choice claims before retrying.

Easy.q: Where does a router read the destination IP address?
o: In the packet header added by the sender.
In the arriving frame’s source MAC field.
In its own interface address instead of the packet.
Easy.h: Review the explanation of this role or action in the lesson. Compare what each choice claims before retrying.

Easy.q: Several installed routes match. Which wins?
o: The most specific matching address group.
The least specific matching address group.
The default route even when a more specific route matches.
Easy.h: Review the explanation of this role or action in the lesson. Compare what each choice claims before retrying.

Easy.q: Who chooses the next connection at each routed hop?
o: The first router chooses every later router’s output port.
Each router checks its own routing table.
The packet chooses a path without consulting a router.
Easy.h: Review the explanation of this role or action in the lesson. Compare what each choice claims before retrying.

Easy.q: What follows the server processing the request?
o: The home router creates the requested webpage.
The request is forwarded unchanged instead of producing a response.
Response packets return for the laptop to process.
Easy.h: Review the explanation of this role or action in the lesson. Compare what each choice claims before retrying.

Hard.q: Inspect ipconfig and tracert example.com on your own Windows PC without changing settings.
o: A timeout does not by itself prove a broken route. If browsing works, some traffic reaches the service; record the missing probe response separately from application success.
Check the correct LAN interface, address/mask, and up/up state. Repair the interface fault rather than adding a redundant route blindly.
Source addressing, NAT, return routes, and interface ACLs can differ. Test from the actual PC and inspect both source-specific paths.
Hard.h: Routers are not required to answer every diagnostic probe.

Hard.q: Before adding a static route to a directly attached LAN, what should you inspect?
o: Repeated failure of the intended application with known-good DNS/service, missing or incorrect routes, unreachable next hops, or interface evidence supports investigation. Asterisks alone do not establish the fault.
Check the correct LAN interface, address/mask, and up/up state. Repair the interface fault rather than adding a redundant route blindly.
A: ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.2. B: ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.1. PCs use their own LAN router addresses as gateways. Interfaces and local routes must also be working.
Hard.h: Review the worked example: Connected routes depend on operational interface state and addressing.

Hard.q: Which routing tables must be checked in a three-router path?
o: Yes, it is in 192.168.8.0/24; it must actually be assigned to the intended router and reachable.
Compare PC mask/subnet and default gateway with the actual LAN router configuration. Then check routing and policy based on results.
Check every router on the request path and the reply path, not only the source gateway; validate next-hop reachability too.
Hard.h: Review the worked example: A’s default route alone cannot give B a missing route.

Hard.q: A PC reaches its neighbor but no remote subnet. Compare two settings first.
o: .5.25 is local; .6.25 is remote and needs the default gateway. A gateway is not needed solely for communication inside the same subnet.
Check host gateway, router routes/next hop, translation match/state, interface policy, upstream reachability, and the return path. Do not treat a NAT rule as proof of routing.
Compare PC mask/subnet and default gateway with the actual LAN router configuration. Then check routing and policy based on results.
Hard.h: Review the worked example: Remote traffic goes to the wrong next hop while local peers may still work.

Hard.q: Can a router connect two private LANs while its WAN cable is unplugged?
o: Yes, if those LAN interfaces and routes work. Reaching the public internet additionally requires the provider/upstream path and supporting settings.
Yes, it is in 192.168.8.0/24; it must actually be assigned to the intended router and reachable.
Compare PC mask/subnet and default gateway with the actual LAN router configuration. Then check routing and policy based on results.
Hard.h: Review the worked example: Routing means forwarding between networks; it is not synonymous with internet service.

Hard.q:
ipconfig shows gateway 192.168.1.1; tracert shows it first, then an asterisk on a later hop while browsing succeeds.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?
o: The /24 mask puts both local devices in 192.168.1.0/24.
The router may use a different source address and bypass a host-facing policy.
The first responding hop often identifies the local router.
Hard.h: Routers are not required to answer every diagnostic probe.

Hard.q:
A router LAN interface is down and its connected route is absent.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?
o: A’s default route alone cannot give B a missing route.
The first responding hop often identifies the local router.
Connected routes depend on operational interface state and addressing.
Hard.h: Review the worked example: Connected routes depend on operational interface state and addressing.

Hard.q:
A → B → server requires B to know the server LAN.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?
o: A’s default route alone cannot give B a missing route.
Remote traffic goes to the wrong next hop while local peers may still work.
The host delivers locally rather than asking the gateway to route the packet.
Hard.h: Review the worked example: A’s default route alone cannot give B a missing route.

Hard.q:
A PC’s configured gateway differs from the local router interface.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?
o: Remote traffic goes to the wrong next hop while local peers may still work.
The /24 mask puts both local devices in 192.168.1.0/24.
The gateway is another reachable host address on its local subnet.
Hard.h: Review the worked example: Remote traffic goes to the wrong next hop while local peers may still work.

Hard.q:
Two lab LANs route successfully with no ISP connection.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?
o: Diagnostic responses and forwarding behavior are separate observations.
Routing means forwarding between networks; it is not synonymous with internet service.
The default route handles destinations without a more specific match.
Hard.h: Review the worked example: Routing means forwarding between networks; it is not synonymous with internet service.

Hard.q: During a lab handover, someone asks: Does a default gateway have to be the website’s address? Which explanation should you give?
o: No. It is the local router address your device uses to reach other networks.
No. Test the failure and verify that routing or switching uses a working alternative correctly.
No. Two uses would make it ambiguous where the omitted zero groups belong.
Hard.h: Separate the roles described in the lesson before drawing a conclusion.

Hard.q: You are explaining this topic to a colleague. Your destination is outside your subnet. Where does your device normally send the packet first?
o: Directly to the destination using its remote MAC address.
To a DNS server for forwarding.
To its default gateway.
Hard.h: Correct. The local gateway is the next hop for destinations outside the subnet when a suitable more-specific route is absent.

Very Hard.q: On paper, use LAN A 192.168.10.0/24, LAN B 192.168.20.0/24, transit A 10.0.0.1/30 and B 10.0.0.2/30. Supply reciprocal routes.
o: The router cannot forward through a known route to that destination and normally drops the packet, potentially generating an unreachable message.
Check every router on the request path and the reply path, not only the source gateway; validate next-hop reachability too.
Yes, it is in 192.168.8.0/24; it must actually be assigned to the intended router and reachable.
A: ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.2. B: ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.1. PCs use their own LAN router addresses as gateways. Interfaces and local routes must also be working.
Very Hard.h: Each next hop is the other router on the transit link.

Very Hard.q: Audit a /30 transit .1/.2 where a remote route points to .6.
o: A timeout does not by itself prove a broken route. If browsing works, some traffic reaches the service; record the missing probe response separately from application success.
The router cannot forward through a known route to that destination and normally drops the packet, potentially generating an unreachable message.
Check the correct LAN interface, address/mask, and up/up state. Repair the interface fault rather than adding a redundant route blindly.
For a directly connected 10.0.0.0/30 transit, .6 is not the peer .2. Use the actual adjacent next hop unless another valid recursive route deliberately reaches .6.
Very Hard.h: Review the worked example: The router must resolve/reach its next hop through valid routing and link information.

Very Hard.q: List the independent checks for a translated outbound connection.
o: Source addressing, NAT, return routes, and interface ACLs can differ. Test from the actual PC and inspect both source-specific paths.
Compare PC mask/subnet and default gateway with the actual LAN router configuration. Then check routing and policy based on results.
Yes, if those LAN interfaces and routes work. Reaching the public internet additionally requires the provider/upstream path and supporting settings.
Check host gateway, router routes/next hop, translation match/state, interface policy, upstream reachability, and the return path. Do not treat a NAT rule as proof of routing.
Very Hard.h: Review the worked example: Translation and routing solve different jobs; translation cannot supply a missing path.

Very Hard.q: Why is router ping not a complete validation of a PC path?
o: Yes, it is in 192.168.8.0/24; it must actually be assigned to the intended router and reachable.
Compare PC mask/subnet and default gateway with the actual LAN router configuration. Then check routing and policy based on results.
Source addressing, NAT, return routes, and interface ACLs can differ. Test from the actual PC and inspect both source-specific paths.

Repeated failure of the intended application with known-good DNS/service, missing or incorrect routes, unreachable next hops, or interface evidence supports investigation. Asterisks alone do not establish the fault.
Very Hard.h: Review the worked example: The router may use a different source address and bypass a host-facing policy.

Very Hard.q: What additional evidence supports a real routing fault rather than probe filtering?
o: A physical access conversion role does not establish routing between IP networks. Integrated equipment can do both, but the roles remain distinct.
Source addressing, NAT, return routes, and interface ACLs can differ. Test from the actual PC and inspect both source-specific paths.

Repeated failure of the intended application with known-good DNS/service, missing or incorrect routes, unreachable next hops, or interface evidence supports investigation. Asterisks alone do not establish the fault.
The router cannot forward through a known route to that destination and normally drops the packet, potentially generating an unreachable message.
Very Hard.h: Review the worked example: Diagnostic responses and forwarding behavior are separate observations.

Very Hard.q:
Router A reaches LAN B, but PC replies fail because Router B has no route to LAN A.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?
o: The outward packet and return packet each require routing decisions.
A’s default route alone cannot give B a missing route.
The router must resolve/reach its next hop through valid routing and link information.
The first responding hop often identifies the local router.
Very Hard.h: Each next hop is the other router on the transit link.

Very Hard.q:
A static route points at a neighbor address outside the connected transit subnet.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?
o: A’s default route alone cannot give B a missing route.
The router must resolve/reach its next hop through valid routing and link information.
The gateway is another reachable host address on its local subnet.
The outward packet and return packet each require routing decisions.
Very Hard.h: Review the worked example: The router must resolve/reach its next hop through valid routing and link information.

Very Hard.q:
Private hosts fail remotely despite a translation rule.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?
o: The ONT handles the optical access link; routing is a separate function.
Translation and routing solve different jobs; translation cannot supply a missing path.
Diagnostic responses and forwarding behavior are separate observations.
Routing means forwarding between networks; it is not synonymous with internet service.
Very Hard.h: Review the worked example: Translation and routing solve different jobs; translation cannot supply a missing path.

Very Hard.q:
A router-originated ping works, but traffic from its LAN host fails.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?
o: The first responding hop often identifies the local router.
The router may use a different source address and bypass a host-facing policy.
The router must resolve/reach its next hop through valid routing and link information.
The outward packet and return packet each require routing decisions.
Very Hard.h: Review the worked example: The router may use a different source address and bypass a host-facing policy.

Very Hard.q:
Several hops do not answer probes, but a service works.
Which explanation is supported by these facts?

learn: Keep one record per row and consistent column headers.
Distinguish numeric values from identifier text.
Preserve leading zeros before entering codes.
Explain stored values versus number formats.
Display percentages and dates intentionally.
Use readable headings, widths and wrapping without hiding data.

sections.title: Give every value a clear job
sections.text: Use a small staff-expense register. Each row describes one expense, while each column answers one question: who, which item, how many or how much? Keep headings in the first row and avoid merging cells inside the list. A decorative merged title can make later selection and analysis harder.
sections.example: An expense row should not mix a staff name, cost and date inside one cell. Put them in separate columns with descriptive headers.
sections.tryIt: Look at the sample list. Explain what one row represents and what Quantity means.
sections.answer: One row is one purchase record. Quantity is the number of units bought, not the amount paid.

sections.title: Numbers and text are different
sections.text: A quantity or cost is usually a number because you may calculate with it. A staff code such as 0017 is an identifier, even though it contains digits. Format an identifier column as Text before entering or pasting codes. Formatting it after Excel has already removed zeros cannot reliably recover the original code.
sections.example: 0017 and 17 can represent different codes. Protect the original text rather than guessing how many zeros were lost.
sections.tryIt: Create a Staff code column, format its empty cells as Text, and enter 0017.
sections.answer: The code should retain both leading zeros. Text is appropriate for an identifier you do not intend to add or multiply.

sections.title: Formatting changes the display
sections.text: A number format normally changes how a value appears, not the value used in a calculation. You can display 12.345 as 12.35 with two decimal places, but calculations still use 12.345. If a business rule requires actual rounding, that requires a rounding calculation, which we cover in a later topic.
sections.example: Displaying 250 as $250.00 does not multiply it or convert its currency. A currency symbol is a label, not an exchange-rate calculation.
sections.tryIt: Enter 12.345 in an empty numeric cell and display two decimal places. Check the formula bar.
sections.answer: The cell can show 12.35 while the formula bar still shows 12.345.

sections.title: Percentages need the right underlying value
sections.text: Percentage formatting displays a value multiplied by 100 followed by %. To represent fifteen percent, enter 15% directly or enter 0.15 and apply Percentage. If you enter 15 first and then apply Percentage, Excel displays 1500%. That display is consistent with the underlying value; it is not a software fault.
sections.example: A discount rate of 0.15 represents 15%. Changing the number of displayed decimal places does not fix an incorrectly entered rate of 15.
sections.tryIt: Enter 0.15 in one cell and 15 in another. Format both as Percentage.
sections.answer: The cells show 15% and 1500%, respectively. Correct the entered value when the intended rate is fifteen percent.

sections.title: Dates and readability
sections.text: Excel can interpret typed dates according to regional settings. A value such as 03/04/2026 is ambiguous across regions. Enter a date deliberately, then apply a clear date format with the month written out, and verify the result. Widen columns, use Wrap Text for long headings and keep the original values visible.
sections.example: 03 Apr 2026 makes the intended day and month clearer than 03/04/2026. A column displaying hashes can need more width; inspect the actual value rather than deleting it.
sections.tryIt: Widen a narrow date column and apply a format that shows a month name.
sections.answer: Confirm the displayed date is the intended date. Width changes presentation, not the underlying date.

sections.title: Check the data before polishing it
sections.text: Before choosing colours, verify records, codes and units. Then use a bold header, consistent numeric formats and enough column width. Keep a clean original copy when experimenting. Good formatting helps a reader understand correct data; it cannot repair missing records, incorrect codes or misleading headings.
sections.example: A neat total in a currency colour scheme is still wrong if the quantity was entered into the Unit cost column.
sections.tryIt: Compare every sample row with its source, then improve the heading and number formats.
sections.answer: The values and record relationships should remain unchanged after formatting. Your identifiers should still retain their zeros.

lab.title: Lab: Clean data and readable sheets
lab.tools: Microsoft Excel (desktop or web), or any spreadsheet app
steps: Start a new sheet and format A2:A4 as Text before pasting the sample into A1:D4.
Apply bold headings, readable widths and a two-decimal numeric or currency format to Unit cost.
In F2 enter 12.345 and display two decimals; explain why the formula bar differs.
In F3 enter 0.15 and apply Percentage; verify 15%.
Add a clearly displayed date, then save an .xlsx copy and verify codes, dates and values after reopening.
lab.check: You can explain why a value and its display can differ, and protect identifiers before entering them.

learn: Start a formula with = and use cell references.
Calculate a line total with multiplication.
Add a contiguous range with SUM.
Distinguish relative, absolute and mixed references.
Copy a formula while keeping a shared rate fixed.
Verify a formula by changing a source value.

sections.title: Let the workbook do the calculation
sections.text: We will calculate purchase costs from the first lesson’s sample. A formula begins with =. Instead of typing the answer yourself, refer to cells containing the inputs. This lets Excel recalculate when those inputs change, provided calculation settings permit it.
sections.example: In D2 enter =B2*C2. With quantity 3 and unit cost 250, the result is 750.
sections.tryIt: Enter the formula in D2, then read the formula bar.
sections.answer: The cell displays 750; the formula bar shows =B2*C2. The formula and the displayed result are different things.

sections.title: Copying relative references
sections.text: Ordinary references such as B2 and C2 are relative. Copying the formula down one row changes them to B3 and C3. This is useful: each row should use its own quantity and price. Copy or fill D2 down to D4, then inspect each resulting formula.
sections.example: D3 becomes =B3*C3 and returns 1000. D4 becomes =B4*C4 and returns 3600.
sections.tryIt: Fill the formula down, then click D4 and check its references.
sections.answer: D4 must use B4 and C4. If every row uses B2 and C2, you have fixed references that should have moved.

sections.title: Add the line totals
sections.text: SUM adds values in a range. In D5 enter =SUM(D2:D4). The colon means the range includes both endpoints. A grand total should include every intended line once and should not include its own result cell.
sections.example: 750 + 1000 + 3600 = 5350. =SUM(D2:D4) returns that amount for the starting data.
sections.tryIt: Calculate D5, then explain why =SUM(D2:D3) would be incomplete.
sections.answer: D2:D3 omits the paper pack. Including D5 in its own total can create a circular reference.

sections.title: Keep a shared rate fixed
sections.text: Put a practice surcharge rate of 10% in H2. This is an invented training rate, not a tax rate or financial recommendation. In E2 enter =D2*$H$2 to calculate that row’s surcharge. The dollar signs fix both the column H and row 2 when the formula is copied.
sections.example: Copy E2 down: E3 becomes =D3*$H$2. The row total moves, while the shared rate remains H2.
sections.tryIt: Fill E2 down to E4 and inspect E4.
sections.answer: E4 should use =D4*$H$2. The surcharges are 75, 100 and 360 for the starting data.

sections.title: Read the dollar signs precisely
sections.text: $H$2 fixes both parts of the reference. H$2 fixes row 2 but lets the column change when copied sideways. $H2 fixes column H but lets the row change when copied downward. H2 fixes neither. The dollar signs control copying; they do not lock a cell against someone editing it.
sections.example: Moving =B2*$H$2 one row down gives =B3*$H$2. Moving it one column right gives =C2*$H$2.
sections.tryIt: Explain which part stays fixed in H$2 and $H2.
sections.answer: H$2 keeps row 2 fixed. $H2 keeps column H fixed. $H$2 keeps both fixed.

sections.title: Test the result instead of trusting the appearance
sections.text: Change Notebook quantity in B2 from 3 to 4. D2 should become 1000 and the grand total should become 5600. Restore the original 3 afterward. Inspect formulas if results fail to update: check references, whether the entry is a formula rather than text, and the calculation setting.
sections.example: Typing 750 as a fixed answer in D2 would not respond when B2 changes. A formula linked to the correct inputs should respond.
sections.tryIt: Perform the change-and-restore check, then save your workbook.
sections.answer: The starting total is 5350, the changed total is 5600, and restoring B2 to 3 restores 5350.

lab.title: Lab: Formulas that survive copying
lab.tools: Microsoft Excel (desktop or web), or any spreadsheet app
steps: Paste the sample into A1:E4 and put Practice surcharge rate in H1 and 10% in H2.
Enter =B2*C2 in D2 and fill down to D4.
Enter =SUM(D2:D4) in D5. Expect 5350.
Enter =D2*$H$2 in E2 and fill down to E4. Expect 75,100,360.
Change B2 to4: expect D2=1000 and D5=5600. Restore3, verify5350, save and reopen.
lab.check: Every copied row uses its own inputs, the shared rate stays fixed, and a changed quantity changes the total correctly.

sources.label: Microsoft: Relative, absolute and mixed references

learn: Explain what a function, an argument and a range are.
Total a range with SUM and average it with AVERAGE.
Find the smallest and largest values with MIN and MAX.
Count numbers with COUNT and non-empty cells with COUNTA.
Spot numbers stored as text that functions ignore.
Check a function result against a quick manual calculation.

sections.title: What a function is
sections.text: A function is a ready-made calculation with a name. You write its name, an opening bracket, the information it needs (its arguments) and a closing bracket. The information is often a range, such as D2:D6. We will use the stationery purchases from earlier lessons, now with two more rows.
sections.example: =SUM(D2:D6) adds the five line totals 750, 1000, 3600, 1200 and 900. The result is 7450.
sections.tryIt: Paste the sample into A1:D6 with Line total in column D, then enter =SUM(D2:D6) in D7.
sections.answer: D7 shows 7450. The formula bar shows =SUM(D2:D6), while the cell shows only the result.

sections.title: The average
sections.text: AVERAGE adds the numbers in a range and divides by how many numbers there are. It ignores empty cells and text, but it does count zeros. An average is pulled towards extreme values, so one very large cost can make it look higher than most items.
sections.example: =AVERAGE(C2:C6) for unit costs 250, 100, 1800, 1200 and 75 returns 685, even though three of the five items cost 250 or less.
sections.tryIt: Enter =AVERAGE(B2:B6) for the quantities and say what it means.
sections.answer: It returns 5.6: the quantities 3, 10, 2, 1 and 12 add to 28, and 28 divided by 5 is 5.6.

sections.title: Smallest and largest
sections.text: MIN returns the smallest number in a range and MAX returns the largest. They tell you the extremes quickly and help you spot entries that look wrong, such as a unit cost of 18000 where 1800 was meant.
sections.example: =MAX(C2:C6) returns 1800 and =MIN(C2:C6) returns 75.
sections.tryIt: Use MAX and MIN on the Quantity column.
sections.answer: MAX(B2:B6) is 12 and MIN(B2:B6) is 1.

sections.title: Counting with COUNT and COUNTA
sections.text: COUNT counts cells that contain numbers. COUNTA counts cells that are not empty, including text. COUNTBLANK counts empty cells. Choose by asking what you want to count: numbers, filled cells or gaps.
sections.example: The item names in A2:A6 are text, so =COUNT(A2:A6) returns 0 but =COUNTA(A2:A6) returns 5.
sections.tryIt: Count the numbers in B2:B6 and the filled cells in A2:A6.
sections.answer: COUNT(B2:B6) returns 5 and COUNTA(A2:A6) returns 5. They are equal here only because no cell is empty.

sections.title: When a number is really text
sections.text: A value that looks like a number can be stored as text, for example when it was pasted with a leading apostrophe. SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT ignore text in a range, so the result is quietly too small. A small green triangle in the cell corner or left-aligned numbers are common warning signs.
sections.example: If the quantity 12 for the folder is stored as text, =SUM(B2:B6) returns 16 instead of 28 and =COUNT(B2:B6) returns 4 instead of 5.
sections.tryIt: Retype 12 in B6 as normal number entry and compare the totals.
sections.answer: With a true number, SUM is 28 and COUNT is 5. A total that is lower than expected often means a number was stored as text.

sections.title: Check before you trust
sections.text: A formula can be correct in form and still give the wrong answer if the range is too short or too long. Check by selecting the range and reading the status bar, which shows the sum, average and count of the selection, and by adding a few cells in your head. Some regional settings use a semicolon between arguments instead of a comma.
sections.example: If =SUM(D2:D5) leaves out the folder row, it returns 6550 instead of 7450. The status bar for D2:D6 shows 7450 straight away.
sections.tryIt: Select D2:D6 and compare the status bar with your formula.
sections.answer: They should match at 7450. If they differ, the formula range is wrong or a value is stored as text.

lab.title: Lab: Summarise a purchase list
lab.tools: Microsoft Excel (desktop or web), or any spreadsheet app
steps: Paste the sample into A1:D6.
In D7 enter =SUM(D2:D6). Expect 7450.
In F1:F4 enter =AVERAGE(B2:B6), =MAX(C2:C6), =MIN(C2:C6) and =COUNTA(A2:A6). Expect 5.6, 1800, 75 and 5.
Select D2:D6 and compare the status bar with D7.
Change B6 to a number stored as text, note how COUNT(B2:B6) changes, then restore it as a number.
lab.check: Every summary matches the expected value and you can explain why COUNT and COUNTA differ.

learn: Turn a range into an Excel Table and name it.
Explain why a table needs a header row and no blank rows.
Sort a table by one column and by two columns.
Filter a table to show only matching rows.
Explain that filtering hides rows and does not delete them.
Add a total row and use a structured reference.

sections.title: From a range to a table
sections.text: A list with headings in the first row, one record per row and no blank rows or columns can become an Excel Table. Click inside the list and choose Insert, then Table, or press Ctrl+T, and confirm that the table has headers. A table adds filter buttons to the headings and grows when you type directly beneath it.
sections.example: The purchases list with Item, Category, Quantity, Unit cost and Line total in A1:E6 becomes a table with five columns and five records.
sections.tryIt: Paste the sample into A1:E6 and turn it into a table with headers.
sections.answer: The headings gain filter arrows and the rows are banded. The table name appears under Table Design.

sections.title: Name the table
sections.text: Excel gives a table a default name such as Table1. Rename it to something meaningful, such as Purchases, in the Table Name box. A clear name makes formulas easier to read and prevents mix-ups when a workbook has several tables.
sections.example: Renaming Table1 to Purchases lets a formula refer to Purchases[Quantity] instead of a range of cell addresses.
sections.tryIt: Rename your table to Purchases.
sections.answer: The Table Name box shows Purchases. Table names cannot contain spaces.

sections.title: Sorting keeps records together
sections.text: Sorting rearranges whole rows, so each record stays together. Use the filter arrow on a heading and choose Sort Smallest to Largest or Largest to Smallest. In a plain range, select the whole list first, otherwise only one column may be rearranged and the records are scrambled.
sections.example: Sorting by Unit cost from largest to smallest gives Paper pack 1800, Stapler 1200, Notebook 250, Pen 100 and Folder 75, each with its own quantity.
sections.tryIt: Sort the table by Unit cost from largest to smallest.
sections.answer: Paper pack comes first with quantity 2. Check that every row still has its own quantity.

sections.title: Sort by more than one column
sections.text: A sort with two levels first orders by one column and then orders ties by another. Use Custom Sort, choose the first column, then add a level. This is useful when many rows share the same category.
sections.example: Sort by Category A to Z, then by Unit cost largest to smallest. Equipment (Stapler) comes first, then Paper (Paper pack, Folder), then Stationery (Notebook, Pen), keeping that order inside each group.
sections.tryIt: Apply the two-level sort and read the order.
sections.answer: The order is Stapler, Paper pack, Folder, Notebook, Pen.

sections.title: Filtering shows only what you ask for
sections.text: A filter hides rows that do not match. The hidden rows are not deleted and their data is still in the file. The row numbers of a filtered list turn blue and some rows are missing from the sequence. Clear the filter to see everything again.
sections.example: Filtering Category to Paper shows only Paper pack and Folder, which are rows 4 and 6 of the sheet. Rows 2, 3 and 5 are hidden.
sections.tryIt: Filter Category to Paper, then clear the filter.
sections.answer: Two rows show while the filter is on and all five come back when it is cleared.

sections.title: Total row and structured references
sections.text: Turn on Total Row in Table Design to add a row at the bottom with a drop-down of summaries. Inside a table, a formula can refer to a column by name. In a row, [@Quantity] means the Quantity value in that same row.
sections.example: In Line total, =[@Quantity]*[@[Unit cost]] gives 750 for the notebook. The total row sum of Quantity is 28.
sections.tryIt: Turn on the total row and show the Sum of Quantity.
sections.answer: The total row shows 28. When you add a new record the table grows and the total includes it.

lab.title: Lab: Table, sort and filter
lab.tools: Microsoft Excel (desktop or web), or any spreadsheet app
steps: Paste the sample into A1:E6 and create a table named Purchases.
Sort by Unit cost largest to smallest. Expect Paper pack first.
Sort by Category A to Z, then Unit cost largest to smallest. Expect Stapler, Paper pack, Folder, Notebook, Pen.
Filter Category to Paper. Expect Paper pack and Folder only, then clear the filter.
Turn on Total Row and show Sum of Quantity. Expect 28.
lab.check: Every record keeps its own values after sorting, the filter hides and restores rows, and the total row shows 28.

learn: Write an IF formula with a test, a true result and a false result.
Combine tests with AND and OR.
Use comparison operators correctly, including <> for not equal.
Recognise #DIV/0!, #NAME?, #VALUE!, #REF! and #N/A.
Use IFERROR sensibly and explain when it hides a real fault.
Test a decision formula on values at the boundary.

sections.title: A formula that decides
sections.text: IF checks a test and returns one result if the test is true and another if it is false. Its pattern is IF(test, result if true, result if false). Text results go inside double quotation marks. We will flag items that are running low using the purchase sample.
sections.example: For the rule "reorder when the quantity is 2 or fewer", enter =IF(B2<=2,"Reorder","OK"). The notebook, with quantity 3, returns OK.
sections.tryIt: Enter the formula in E2 and fill it down to E6.
sections.answer: The results are OK, OK, Reorder, Reorder and OK for notebook, pen, paper pack, stapler and folder.

sections.title: Comparison operators
sections.text: A test compares two things. The operators are = equal, <> not equal, > greater than, < less than, >= greater than or equal and <= less than or equal. Test the boundary carefully: the difference between < 2 and <= 2 decides what happens when the value is exactly 2.
sections.example: With <2 the paper pack (quantity 2) would not be flagged; with <=2 it is. The stapler (1) is flagged by both.
sections.tryIt: Change the formula to B2<2 and see which items change.
sections.answer: Only the stapler is flagged. The paper pack changes from Reorder to OK.

sections.title: Combine tests with AND and OR
sections.text: AND returns TRUE only when every test is true. OR returns TRUE when at least one test is true. Put them inside the IF test to build a richer rule. Brackets and commas must match, so build the formula in small steps.
sections.example: =IF(AND(B2<=2,C2>1500),"Urgent","Check") returns Urgent for the paper pack (quantity 2, cost 1800) and Check for the stapler (quantity 1, cost 1200).
sections.tryIt: Enter the AND formula in F2 and fill it down.
sections.answer: Only the paper pack is Urgent. The others are Check.

sections.title: Reading the common errors
sections.text: An error value tells you what kind of problem Excel found. #DIV/0! means dividing by zero or an empty cell. #NAME? means Excel does not recognise a name, often a mistyped function or unquoted text. #VALUE! means the wrong type of value, such as text in a calculation. #REF! means a referenced cell was deleted. #N/A means a value is not available, which is common with lookups.
sections.example: If the quantity were 0, =D2/B2 would return #DIV/0!. Typing =SUMM(D2:D6) returns #NAME?.
sections.tryIt: Set B2 to 0 temporarily and enter =D2/B2 in G2. Then restore B2 to 3.
sections.answer: G2 shows #DIV/0! while B2 is 0. Restoring 3 gives 250.

sections.title: IFERROR, used with care
sections.text: IFERROR(value, value if error) shows a friendlier result when a formula gives an error. It is useful for a known harmless case, such as a cost per unit when no units were bought. It can also hide real mistakes, such as a deleted cell, so use it where you understand the cause.
sections.example: =IFERROR(D2/B2,"No units") shows No units instead of #DIV/0! when B2 is 0. If a reference had been deleted, it would also show No units, which would be misleading.
sections.tryIt: Wrap the division in IFERROR and test with B2 set to 0, then restore 3.
sections.answer: The cell shows No units at 0 and 250 at 3. Restoring the data confirms the formula itself works.

sections.title: Test the edges
sections.text: A decision formula is only as good as its tests. Try values on each side of every boundary and an unusual case such as an empty cell or text. If the quantity cell is empty, B2<=2 treats it as 0 and returns Reorder, which might not be what you want.
sections.example: Test quantities 1, 2 and 3 for the rule B2<=2: they return Reorder, Reorder and OK.
sections.tryIt: Type 1, 2 and 3 into B2 in turn, then restore 3.
sections.answer: Quantities 1 and 2 give Reorder and 3 gives OK. Restore the original value afterwards.

lab.title: Lab: Decisions and errors
lab.tools: Microsoft Excel (desktop or web), or any spreadsheet app
steps: Paste the sample into A1:D6.
In E2 enter =IF(B2<=2,"Reorder","OK") and fill down. Expect OK, OK, Reorder, Reorder, OK.
In F2 enter =IF(AND(B2<=2,C2>1500),"Urgent","Check") and fill down. Expect only the paper pack as Urgent.
Set B2 to 0, enter =D2/B2 in G2 and note #DIV/0!. Wrap it in IFERROR with the text No units.
Restore B2 to 3 and confirm G2 returns 250.
lab.check: Each decision formula matches the rule on boundary values and you can explain what each error value means.

sources.label: Microsoft: Hide error values and error indicators in cells

Easy.q: What should one row represent in the taught purchase list?
o: Every purchase by every person together
One complete purchase record
A separate application account
One font choice
Easy.h: A row groups the fields belonging to the same record.

Easy.q: How should you protect a staff code 0017 before entering it?
o: Apply Percentage after typing 17
Format the empty identifier cells as Text
Round it to two decimals
Multiply it by 100
Easy.h: Formatting as Text before entry preserves the identifier characters.

Easy.q: What does number formatting normally change?
o: The number of worksheet tabs
How a stored value is displayed
The record owner
The actual exchange rate
Easy.h: A display format generally leaves the value used for calculation unchanged.

Easy.q: Which stored numeric value displays as 15% with Percentage format?
Easy.h: Percentage display multiplies the underlying value by 100.

Easy.q: Which date presentation is least ambiguous to readers in different regions?
o: A bare number 03
The text this month
03/04/2026 without explanation
Easy.h: Writing the month name makes the intended month explicit.

Easy.q: What should you do if a heading is too long for its column?
o: Delete the heading’s last words
Adjust the width or use Wrap Text
Replace the heading with a cost value
Change every record into a title
Easy.h: Readability can improve without removing information.

Hard.q: Your staff code 0017 becomes 17 after numeric entry. What prevents this for future codes?
o: Set the empty code column to Text before pasting
Increase the currency decimal places
Apply 15% formatting to the code
Use a wider column only
Hard.h: Width and numeric formats do not preserve the original identifier text at entry.

Hard.q: A cell holds 12.345 and shows 12.35. Which statement is accurate?
o: Excel has multiplied the value by 100
The original value is always destroyed
The cell must contain text
The two-decimal display has not necessarily rounded the stored value
Hard.h: Check the formula bar: the original precision can remain.

Hard.q: A rate entered as 15 now displays 1500%. What should you correct?
o: The workbook extension
The underlying rate to 0.15 or enter 15% directly
Only the number of decimal places
Only the font size
Hard.h: The percentage format is displaying the entered value consistently.

Hard.q: A cost displays$250.00 instead of 250. What happened?
o: The numeric value became 25000
The quantity was added automatically
A currency display format was applied
A foreign-exchange conversion was calculated
Hard.h: A symbol does not perform currency conversion.

Hard.q: You must preserve a long numeric-looking customer identifier exactly. Best entry type?
o: Text, prepared before entering the identifier
Percentage
A two-decimal cost
A date with a month name
Hard.h: Identifiers are labels; storing them as numbers may alter their representation or precision.

Hard.q: A date column shows hashes after you narrow it. What should you inspect first?
o: Widen the column and verify the actual date value
Delete every affected record
Convert the whole workbook to an image
Change the date to today without checking
Hard.h: An insufficient display width is a common cause; inspect before changing data.

Hard.q: A list contains an item and quantity inside the same field. Why separate them?
o: Because every cell must hold exactly five characters
Each column should have one clear meaning
Because worksheets cannot contain numbers
Because text cannot appear in Excel
Hard.h: Separate fields support readable and reliable data entry.

Hard.q: A formatted heading is neat, but quantities and costs were swapped. What takes priority?
o: Hide both columns permanently
Save asCSV to repair the values
Correct the data and field placement before styling
Add a brighter heading colour
Hard.h: Presentation does not repair incorrect data.

Hard.q: You enter 0.075 and apply Percentage with one decimal. What display should you expect?
Hard.h: 0.075 multiplied by 100 gives 7.5 percent.

Hard.q: A date 03/04/2026 was interpreted differently on two systems. What is the safest response?
o: Swap the numbers without asking
Confirm the intended date and use an unambiguous month-name display
Format it as Currency
Assume every system uses the same regional order
Hard.h: Regional date interpretation can differ; confirm meaning before changing it.

Hard.q: Your work list uses merged cells across several data records. What structure fits the lesson?
o: Unmerged field columns with one record per row
A separate colour for every character
One merged cell for all records
No header row
Hard.h: A consistent rectangular list is easier to inspect and extend.

Hard.q: Before submitting the formatted register, what verification matters?
o: Only the chosen theme name
Only whether the file is open
Only whether all borders are identical
Codes, units and values still match the original records
Hard.h: Accuracy and retained meaning come before decoration.

Very Hard.q: You receive code 17 but cannot tell whether the source was 17,017 or 0017. What is defensible?
o: Assume every code must have four digits
Always add exactly two zeros
Convert 17 to 17%
Check the original source instead of inventing the missing zeros
Very Hard.h: Once information is lost, formatting alone cannot establish its original form.

Very Hard.q: Two expenses each store 12.345 and display 12.35. Why might a calculation differ from adding the visible rounded amounts?
o: Calculations can use underlying precision rather than displayed rounding
Currency symbols always add a hidden fee
Every formatted number becomes an integer
A wider column changes arithmetic
Very Hard.h: Displayed decimals and stored values can differ; decide separately whether actual rounding is required.

Very Hard.q: A numeric code must display four digits, but another system needs the exact identifier text. Which approach is safer?
o: Rely only on a custom visual zero format
Apply Currency to the code
Preserve it as text before entry and verify exported data
Multiply every identifier by 1000
Very Hard.h: A display-only format does not guarantee another system receives the intended identifier characters.

Very Hard.q: A manager wants every amount labelledUSD although the source amounts areGYD. What should you explain?
o: Changing the symbol alone does not convert the currency
The USD symbol automatically fetches an exchange rate
Excel assumes all currencies are equal
Decimal formatting converts between currencies
Very Hard.h: Unit labels and currency conversion are different; this lesson does not perform a conversion.

Very Hard.q: A discount is meant to be 15%, but the stored value is 15. Why does changing from 0 to 2 displayed decimals not repair it?
o: The workbook has too many sheets
Formatting can only be applied before saving
It changes display precision, not the underlying rate
Two decimals always erase percentage symbols
Very Hard.h: The underlying value must be corrected to match the intended rate.

Very Hard.q: A phone number starts with 0 and is not used for arithmetic. Which reason supports Text?
o: It preserves identifier characters rather than treating the value as a quantity
Text guarantees the phone is connected
Text adds missing digits from the internet
Text automatically verifies the number exists
Very Hard.h: Text preserves representation; it does not verify the real-world identifier.

Very Hard.q: One person changed 03Aprto 04Mar while trying to improve the date format. What failed?
o: Only the font weight changed
The row count increased automatically
The underlying meaning changed, rather than only its presentation
A CSV file gained two worksheets
Very Hard.h: A formatting task should retain the intended date; confirm both value and display.

Very Hard.q: A quantity column contains both 5 and the text five. What problem should you address before later calculations?
o: Inconsistent data representation in a numeric field
The column letter is too short
All text must be deleted from the workbook
The header must be merged with row 2
Very Hard.h: Consistent field types reduce calculation and interpretation problems.

Very Hard.q: An attractive register hides the last digits of staff codes. What should you change?
o: Make the full codes visible and verify their stored text
Remove the code column’s heading
Approve it because the colour scheme is professional
Replace the codes with rounded costs
Very Hard.h: A reader must be able to inspect identifiers accurately.

Very Hard.q: A colleague says every formatted date is proof the input was correct. Best response?
o: Wider columns fix ambiguous original meaning
Month names stop all entry mistakes
Date formatting validates every source automatically
A plausible date display can still represent the wrong day; compare with the intended source
Very Hard.h: Formatting improves clarity but does not prove correct source interpretation.

Easy.q: Which character normally starts an Excel formula?
Easy.h: The equals sign begins an ordinary formula entry.

Easy.q: Which formula calculates quantity B2 times unit cost C2?
Easy.h: Multiplication calculates quantity times unit cost.

Easy.q: Which formula adds line totalsD2 throughD4?
o: =SUM(D5:D5)
=SUM(D2:D4)
=SUM(D2,D4)
Easy.h: The colon describes the whole inclusive range, not only its endpoints.

Easy.q: Copying=B2*C2 down one row normally produces:
Easy.h: Relative references move with the copied formula.

Easy.q: Which reference fixes both column H and row 2 when copying?
o: H2
Easy.h: A dollar sign before each part fixes that part.

Easy.q: Which test checks that your formula uses its inputs?
o: Change a source quantity and verify the result, then restore it
Replace the formula with its old answer
Rename the worksheet without checking results
Change only the font colour
Easy.h: A controlled input change tests the calculation connection.

Hard.q: Notebook quantity is 3 and cost is 250. What should=B2*C2 return?
Hard.h: Three units at 250 each cost 750.

Hard.q: The next row has quantity 10 and cost 100. After filling D2 down, D3 should be:
o: =B2*C2, returning 750
=D3*D3, returning 0
=B3*C3, returning 1000
=B3+C3, returning 110
Hard.h: Each copied row should use its own input cells.

Hard.q: The three line totals are 750,1000 and 3600. What should the grand total be?
Hard.h: Adding all three totals gives 5350.

Hard.q: Why does=SUM(D2,D4)return 4350 with the sample?
o: It always ignoresD2
It multipliesD2 byD4
It adds only the two listed endpoints and omitsD3
It includes every cell betweenD2 andD4
Hard.h: A comma-separated list and a colon range are different expressions.

Hard.q: A shared practice rate is in H2. Which formula in E2 can be copied down correctly?
Hard.h: The line total should move; the shared rate should not.

Hard.q: Why is a dollar sign in$H$2 not cell protection?
o: It assigns a password to H2
It encrypts the workbook
It makes the cell read-only for all users
It controls reference movement during copying, not permission to editH2
Hard.h: Reference anchoring and worksheet protection are separate features.

Hard.q: Move=B2*$H$2 one column right. What is the copied formula?
Hard.h: The relativeBcolumn moves toC; the absolute rate staysH2.

Hard.q: Move=B2*$H$2 one row down. What is the copied formula?
Hard.h: The relative row moves from 2 to 3; the fixed reference does not.

Hard.q: Which part stays fixed inH$2?
o: Row 2
BothH and 2
Neither part
ColumnH
Hard.h: Only the row has a preceding dollar sign.

Hard.q: Which part stays fixed in$H2?
o: ColumnH
The whole worksheet
The displayed answer
Row 2
Hard.h: Only the column has a preceding dollar sign.

Hard.q: B2 changes from 3 to 4 whileC2 stays 250. What new D2 and grand total are expected?
o: D2=254 and grand total=4854
D2=4000 and grand total=8600
D2=750 and grand total=5350
D2=1000 and grand total=5600
Hard.h: The changed line increases by 250, so 5350 becomes 5600.

Hard.q: D2 contains the typed value 750, not a formula. What happens whenB2 changes?
o: D2 automatically discovers the multiplication
The stored value becomes$H$2
D2 always changes to 1000
D2 does not recalculate from that input
Hard.h: A hard-coded answer is not linked to the input cells.

Very Hard.q: A total in D5 uses=SUM(D2:D5). What is the structural problem?
o: It locks row 5 against editing
It includes its own result cell and can create a circular reference
It calculates onlyD4
It omitsD2
Very Hard.h: A result should not normally depend on itself.

Very Hard.q: Every surcharge row repeats 75 even though the line totals differ. The copied formula is=$D$2*$H$2. What needs changing?
o: Remove every dollar sign from both references
FixD2 and allowH2 to move
Change 75 to a coloured font
Use a relative line-total referenceD2 while keeping$H$2 fixed
Very Hard.h: The calculation wrongly fixes the first line total in every row.

Very Hard.q: E3 uses=D3*H3 after copyingE2. H3 isblank. What caused the shared-rate error?
o: SUM skipped the middle record
The rate reference was relative and moved from H2 to H3
The worksheet filename was incorrect
The multiplication sign changed into addition
Very Hard.h: Fix the shared-rate reference with$H$2 before filling.

Very Hard.q: A practice rate in H2 changes from 10%to 20%. With correct references, what are the three new surcharges?
Very Hard.h: Multiply 750,1000 and 3600 by 0.20.

Very Hard.q: Copy=B2*H$2 one column right. Which result exposes the remaining relative part?

Hard.task: Explain the difference between < and <= for the paper pack.
Hard.answer: The paper pack has quantity 2, so <=2 is true and <2 is false.

Hard.task: What does OR change in the Urgent rule?
Hard.answer: Either test being true flags the item, so the stapler would also be flagged by the quantity test.
Hard.reason: OR needs only one true test.

Very Hard.task: Explain two reasons IFERROR can mislead.
Very Hard.answer: It hides real faults such as deleted references, and a blank result can quietly leave values out of totals.
Very Hard.reason: Know the cause before hiding it.

Very Hard.task: Design three test values for the rule "Reorder when quantity is 2 or fewer".
Very Hard.answer: Use 1, 2 and 3. Expect Reorder, Reorder, OK.
Very Hard.reason: Both sides of the boundary and the boundary.

Very Hard.task: A formula returns #NAME? after you typed =IF(B2<=2,Reorder,"OK"). Find the fault.
Very Hard.answer: Reorder is missing double quotation marks, so Excel reads it as a name.
Very Hard.reason: Text results need quotes.

Very Hard.task: Write a formula that returns Review when B2 is empty and otherwise decides Reorder or OK.
Very Hard.answer: =IF(B2="","Review",IF(B2<=2,"Reorder","OK"))
Very Hard.reason: Test for empty first.

Very Hard.task: Describe how you would check a decision formula before sharing a workbook.
Very Hard.answer: Test boundary and unusual values, check each error case, and restore the original data.
Very Hard.reason: Evidence before trust.
